ultracode: run an adversarial multi-agent review of the michi codebase (current HEAD on `main`, working tree clean). Read CLAUDE.md first for non-negotiables, then docs/00-overview.md and docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-03-michi-design.md for the "why" behind the architecture.

CONTEXT — what michi is and why:
michi is a Rust crate of AXI (Agent eXperience Interface) response primitives — the primitive layer of the orin-axi suite. It's pure-computation rendering (TOON lists, KV items, truncation, empty states, structured errors, status, hints) that four other tools (Monokl, Firkin, Lumen, Pulse) will depend on. Consumed from Rust directly and from TypeScript via a NAPI wrapper (packages/michi-node, npm package "michi").

The core design bet is token efficiency + agent ergonomics without sacrificing human ergonomics — TOON output is ~40% fewer tokens than JSON, help[] blocks give agents concrete next-step paths, errors always render agent-readable text with exit codes. Every architectural and lint decision should be judged against this: does it serve DX (for both human maintainers and LLM callers) and long-term maintainability across the whole suite, not just this one crate.

CURRENT SCOPE (Plan 1 / MVP, v0.1.0, complete):
- Always-compiled, zero-dep rendering: toon/, kv/, hints.rs, truncate.rs, empty.rs, error.rs, idempotency.rs, recovery.rs, status.rs, response.rs, resilience/mod.rs (RetryConfig, next_retry_delay, parse_retry_after), pipeline/mod.rs (pure Pipeline data type + render(), no execution)
- Feature-gated (default = [], zero runtime deps): pipeline (tokio), fuzzy (nucleo-matcher), cache (moka+sha2), cli, mcp, napi
- pipeline/executor.rs, resilience/circuit.rs, resilience/policy.rs, sink/mod.rs are INTENTIONAL STUBS (1-2 lines) for Plan 2 (execution engine) — not yet implemented. Do not flag their absence as a defect; do flag if the feature-gating/module boundary around them is unsound.
- packages/michi-node: thin NAPI v3 cdylib shim (catch_unwind on every export)

NON-NEGOTIABLES (from CLAUDE.md — verify adherence, don't just take my word for it):
- No unwrap()/expect() in lib code (tests OK with a message)
- No unsafe outside the napi boundary
- BTreeMap for output maps (deterministic ordering), HashMap only for internal state
- Strings pre-allocated with String::with_capacity
- Truncation must use char boundaries (floor_char_boundary), never byte-slice blindly
- Every pub item has a doc comment
- NAPI: napi/napi-derive = "3", #[napi(catch_unwind)] on every export, no u64 across the FFI boundary
- Benchmarks use divan, tests use cargo nextest

LINT POSTURE already in place (src/lib.rs, .clippy.toml, .rustfmt.toml): clippy::pedantic + a curated slice of clippy::restriction (unwrap_used, expect_used, panic, todo, unimplemented, indexing_slicing, disallowed_macros, implicit_clone, inefficient_to_string, use_self) warned in the lib crate, several DENIED in packages/michi-node (panics at the FFI boundary crash the host process). 120-char width. This was tuned to be "pedantic as a baseline, minus rules that fight good structure" — the review should sanity-check that calibration, not just rubber-stamp it.

REVIEW DIMENSIONS (adversarial — actively try to find real defects, not just style nits):
1. Rust best-practices adherence — does the actual code live up to the non-negotiables above and idiomatic Rust more broadly (error handling, ownership, API ergonomics, trait design)?
2. Architecture — is the feature-gating actually zero-cost/zero-dep as claimed? Are module boundaries (rendering vs. execution, always-compiled vs. gated) sound and will they hold up as Plan 2 fills in the stubs? Any layering violations or leaky abstractions?
3. Performance — allocation patterns in the hot paths (toon/kv rendering, escape_value, truncate), unnecessary clones, capacity pre-sizing correctness, anything that would matter at the list-rendering scale this crate targets.
4. Security — input handling at the NAPI boundary (untrusted JS values crossing into Rust), integer casts (there was a recent fix for a negative i32→usize wrap in packages/michi-node/src/lib.rs render_toon — check for siblings of that bug), dependency/license posture (deny.toml), anything unsafe.

Also actively look for over-engineering or premature abstraction in the other direction — flag anything that adds ceremony without adding real safety/clarity, since the stated goal is "lint consistently but don't make it hard to write the best possible code," not maximal strictness for its own sake.

Use the Workflow tool with an adversarial-verify pattern: dimension-scoped finders in parallel, each finding independently verified/refuted before being reported, ranked most-severe first. Report file:line, concrete failure scenario, and verdict for each surviving finding.
I'll start by reading the design docs and getting a sense of the repo structure, then author a Workflow script for the adversarial multi-agent review.

1	# michi — Overview
2	
3	> orin-axi · Draft · June 2026
4	
5	---
6	
7	## What it is
8	
9	`michi` is a Rust crate of pure agentic response primitives — the formatting and signalling
10	conventions that make tools ergonomic for LLMs regardless of protocol or language. It is the
11	primitive layer of the **orin-axi** suite, encoding the [AXI](https://axi.md) (Agent eXperience
12	Interface) design principles as typed, tested Rust.
13	
14	AXI is a set of ten design principles for agent-ergonomic tooling that treats token budget as a
15	first-class constraint. Of the ten, michi encodes **seven** directly: TOON list rendering (P1),
16	content truncation (P3), pre-computed aggregates (P4), definitive empty states (P5), structured
17	errors with exit codes (P6), content-first status responses (P8), and contextual disclosure via
18	`help[]` blocks (P9). It also ships supporting idempotency and retry-delay primitives. The
19	remaining three principles (P2, P7, P10) depend on integration that michi deliberately excludes.
20	
21	The crate is intentionally narrow: **no protocol knowledge, no async runtime, no CLI framework**.
22	Pure computation — data in, strings and types out. TypeScript consumers reach it via the NAPI npm
23	wrapper `michi`; Rust consumers take a direct crates.io or git dependency.
24	
25	---
26	
27	## Quick start
28	
29	The same primitives, from either language. (Illustrative — see `docs/01-spec.md` for the precise
30	API.)
31	
32	```rust
33	use michi::toon;
34	
35	#[derive(serde::Serialize)]
36	struct Issue {
37	    number: u64,
38	    title: String,
39	    state: String,
40	}
41	
42	let issues = vec![
43	    Issue { number: 51815, title: "[Bug]: Telegram plugin".into(), state: "open".into() },
44	    Issue { number: 51812, title: "dark mode request".into(), state: "open".into() },
45	];
46	
47	// TOON list, an inline total count, and a next-step hint.
48	let response = toon::list("issues", &issues)
49	    .total(8771)
50	    .hint("gh-axi issue view <number>", "view an issue")
51	    .render();
52	
53	print!("{response}");
54	```
55	
56	```typescript
57	import { toon } from "michi";
58	
59	const issues = [
60	  { number: 51815, title: "[Bug]: Telegram plugin", state: "open" },
61	  { number: 51812, title: "dark mode request", state: "open" },
62	];
63	
64	// Identical primitives, via the NAPI wrapper.
65	const response = toon
66	  .list("issues", issues)
67	  .total(8771)
68	  .hint("gh-axi issue view <number>", "view an issue")
69	  .render();
70	
71	process.stdout.write(response);
72	```
73	
74	Both produce the same token-efficient output:
75	
76	```text
77	count: 2 of 8771 total
78	issues[2]{number,title,state}:
79	  51815,"[Bug]: Telegram plugin",open
80	  51812,dark mode request,open
81	help[1]:
82	  Run `gh-axi issue view <number>` to view an issue
83	```
84	
85	---
86	
87	## Name
88	
89	**michi** — from 道 (Japanese: path, way, road).
90	
91	The character 道 is the root of *dō* in martial arts and traditional arts: judo, kendo, aikido,
92	shodō, chadō. It means the path itself — and the act of travelling it with intention. In the
93	context of this crate, every `help[]` block is michi: a marker that tells an agent which path to
94	take next, with what parameters.
95	
96	Fits the suite's naming aesthetic: short real words borrowed from a specific domain, with a
97	metaphor that earns its place.
98	
99	| Name      | Origin          | Meaning                       |
100	| --------- | --------------- | ----------------------------- |
101	| Lumen     | Latin           | unit of luminous flux; light  |
102	| Firkin    | Middle English  | small barrel; a measured unit |
103	| Monokl    | Slavic / French | monocle; single-eye focus     |
104	| Pulse     | Latin           | vital sign; rhythmic signal   |
105	| **michi** | Japanese (道)   | path, way, road               |
106	
107	---
108	
109	## Organisation
110	
111	GitHub org: **orin-axi** (`github.com/orin-axi`)
112	
113	> "AXI" = Agent eXperience Interface. The orin-axi org is the umbrella for tools designed to serve
114	> both human developers and AI agents as first-class users. `michi` is the primitive layer — the
115	> shared vocabulary of agent responses that all other tools in the suite can build on.
116	
117	---
118	
119	## Where michi fits in the suite
120	
121	michi sits below every other tool in the orin-axi suite as the shared primitive layer. Each
122	agent-facing tool imports it rather than re-implementing AXI formatting.
123	
124	| Tool      | What it does                               | Uses michi for           |
125	| --------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------ |
126	| **michi** | AXI response primitives — the shared layer | — (this crate)           |
127	| Monokl    | AST-based semantic code search             | TOON list output         |
128	| Firkin    | Barrel / index file generator              | Structured error output  |
129	| Lumen     | Coding-session analysis + ambient context  | Status + hint primitives |
130	| Pulse     | Code-health intelligence                   | TOON list output         |
131	
132	Non-agentic infrastructure tools (build scripts, formatters, etc.) never encounter michi — the
133	package boundary enforces the separation.
134	
135	---
136	
137	## AXI principles encoded
138	
139	| Principle                           | Module       | What michi provides                               | Status  |
140	| ----------------------------------- | ------------ | ------------------------------------------------- | ------- |
141	| P1 — Token-efficient output         | `toon`       | TOON list rendering (~40% fewer tokens than JSON) | Encoded |
142	| P2 — Minimal default schemas        | `toon`, `kv` | Compact rendering; field names stated once        | Caller  |
143	| P3 — Content truncation             | `truncate`   | Size-bounded fields with `--full` escape hatch    | Encoded |
144	| P4 — Pre-computed aggregates        | `toon`, `kv` | Inline `totalCount` on every list and item        | Encoded |
145	| P5 — Definitive empty states        | `empty`      | Explicit `count: 0` message — never silent        | Encoded |
146	| P6 — Structured errors & exit codes | `error`      | Typed TOON errors on stdout; clean exit codes     | Encoded |
147	| P7 — Ambient context                | `status`     | `StatusResponse` payload for session dashboards   | Caller  |
148	| P8 — Content first                  | `status`     | Live-state response for no-arg invocations        | Encoded |
149	| P9 — Contextual disclosure          | `hints`      | `help[]` blocks of concrete next-step templates   | Encoded |
150	| P10 — Consistent way to get help    | —            | Per-subcommand `--help` reference contract        | Caller  |
151	
152	michi encodes **seven** principles directly — P1, P3, P4, P5, P6, P8, and P9 — as typed, tested
153	Rust, alongside supporting idempotency and retry-delay primitives (`idempotency`) that underpin
154	P6's robustness guarantees and make combined operations safe to retry.
155	
156	The remaining three are the **caller's responsibility**, because each requires integration michi
157	deliberately omits:
158	
159	- **P2 — Minimal default schemas** — michi renders any schema compactly, but the caller chooses
160	  which fields to expose by default and which to gate behind a `--fields` flag.
161	- **P7 — Ambient context** — michi produces the `StatusResponse` payload, but installing it into
162	  per-session hooks or a plugin system requires a CLI/agent harness.
163	- **P10 — Consistent way to get help** — routing per-subcommand `--help` is a CLI-framework
164	  concern, outside a pure primitives crate.
165	
166	---
167	
168	## Namespaces
169	
170	| Surface                | Name             |
171	| ---------------------- | ---------------- |
172	| Rust crate (crates.io) | `michi`          |
173	| npm package            | `michi`          |
174	| Rust module path       | `michi::`        |
175	| GitHub repo            | `orin-axi/michi` |
176	
177	---
178	
179	## License
180	
181	AGPL v3 (`AGPL-3.0-or-later`).
182	
183	Rationale: viral copyleft is well-suited to CLI/library tools embedded in pipelines. Creates
184	natural friction against agentic services wrapping michi commercially without contributing back. A
185	CLA or contributor copyright assignment clause per repo preserves future dual-licensing
186	optionality.
187	
188	---
189	
190	## Publishing targets
191	
192	- **crates.io** — public, `michi`
193	- **npmjs.com** — public, `michi` (NAPI wrapper)
194	- NAPI binaries cross-compiled via `cargo-zigbuild`:
195	  - `darwin-arm64`
196	  - `linux-x64-musl`
197	
198	---
199	
200	## Documents in this repo
201	
202	| File                      | Contents                                              |
203	| ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
204	| `docs/00-overview.md`     | This file — project identity, naming, suite context   |
205	| `docs/01-spec.md`         | Full technical specification — modules, API, grammar  |
206	| `docs/projects/01-mvp.md` | MVP implementation plan — agent sessions, constraints |
207	
208	---
209	
210	## Open questions
211	
212	See `docs/01-spec.md` § Open questions for the five ADR items that need resolution before or during
213	the MVP build (TOON vs KV retrieval accuracy, consumer strategy, `cli` feature scope, NAPI export
214	surface, recovery hint typing).
215

1	# michi — Architecture Design
2	> orin-axi · 2026-07-03
3	
4	This document records the architectural decisions made during the July 2026
5	brainstorming session. It supersedes and extends any open questions in
6	`01-spec.md` (which predates this session). Implementation plans should treat
7	this doc as authoritative on the topics it covers.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## 1. One crate, feature-gated
12	
13	**Decision: one `michi` crate with optional features. No separate execution crate.**
14	
15	The original spec positioned michi as a pure sync rendering library with no
16	async runtime. The question was whether pipeline execution (tokio, moka, nucleo)
17	should live in a companion crate (`kata`) or in michi itself behind features.
18	
19	Feature gates give the same guarantee that crate boundaries give — a consumer
20	who adds `michi` with default features pulls in zero tokio, zero moka, zero
21	nucleo. The "pure computation" principle is enforced by cargo, not by convention.
22	
23	The suite tools (Monokl, Firkin, Lumen, Pulse) all need both rendering primitives
24	and pipeline execution. One crate means one dep, one version pin, one mental model.
25	Two crates would require cross-crate type conversions and coordinated releases with
26	no architectural benefit.
27	
28	The NAPI wrapper (`packages/michi-node`) remains a separate Cargo crate because
29	`crate-type = ["cdylib"]` cannot coexist with a regular `[lib]` in one
30	`Cargo.toml`. This is a build-artifact boundary, not a conceptual one.
31	
32	---
33	
34	## 2. Feature taxonomy
35	
36	```toml
37	[features]
38	default  = []
39	
40	# Async execution layer: PipelineExecutor, Step, CheckpointStore, OutputSink,
41	# CircuitBreaker, with_resilience(). Adds: tokio, tokio-util, async-trait, uuid.
42	# Note: thiserror and serde are regular (non-optional) deps used by all features.
43	pipeline = [
44	    "dep:tokio",
45	    "dep:tokio-util",
46	    "dep:async-trait",
47	    "dep:uuid",
48	]
49	
50	# Fuzzy matching: FuzzyMatcher, FuzzyResolver, Disambiguator trait.
51	# Implies pipeline (Resolution<T> is used in pipeline context).
52	# Adds: nucleo-matcher.
53	fuzzy = ["dep:nucleo-matcher", "pipeline"]
54	
55	# Two-tier cache: moka async LRU + disk LRU with tag invalidation +
56	# stale-while-revalidate. Adds: moka, sha2.
57	cache = ["dep:moka", "dep:sha2", "pipeline"]
58	
59	# CLI surface adapter: CliSink (indicatif spinners), DiskCheckpointStore,
60	# TtyDisambiguator, install_ctrl_c_handler.
61	# Adds: indicatif, inquire, crossterm, ctrlc, atty.
62	cli = [
63	    "dep:indicatif",
64	    "dep:inquire",
65	    "dep:crossterm",
66	    "dep:ctrlc",
67	    "dep:atty",
68	    "pipeline",
69	]
70	
71	# MCP surface adapter: McpSink, MemoryCheckpointStore, McpDisambiguator.
72	# Pure logic — no additional non-tokio deps.
73	mcp = ["pipeline"]
74	
75	# NAPI npm wrapper surface. Used by packages/michi-node only.
76	napi = ["dep:napi", "dep:napi-derive"]
77	
78	# Everything except napi (napi is build-artifact-level, not feature-level).
79	full = ["pipeline", "fuzzy", "cache", "cli", "mcp"]
80	```
81	
82	Typical consumer configs:
83	
84	| Consumer | Features |
85	|---|---|
86	| Pure rendering (Rust CLI, no pipeline) | `michi` (defaults) |
87	| Rust CLI that runs pipelines | `michi = { features = ["cli"] }` |
88	| TypeScript MCP server via npm | `michi` npm package (default) |
89	| MCP server that runs pipelines | `michi = { features = ["mcp"] }` |
90	| Test/bench harness | `michi = { features = ["full"] }` |
91	| `packages/michi-node` Cargo.toml | `michi = { features = ["napi"] }` |
92	
93	---
94	
95	## 3. Module map
96	
97	Modules in the left column are always compiled (default features). Modules in
98	the right column are gated.
99	
100	```
101	src/
102	  lib.rs
103	
104	  ── Always compiled ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
105	
106	  toon/
107	    mod.rs          render_toon(), ToonOptions, Value
108	    escape.rs       comma/quote/null escaping
109	    render.rs       string assembly with pre-allocated capacity
110	
111	  kv/
112	    mod.rs          render_kv(), KvItem, KvValue
113	
114	  hints.rs          Hint, render_hints(), append_hints()
115	  truncate.rs       Truncated, truncate(), truncate_inline()
116	  empty.rs          empty_state(), empty_state_with_hints()
117	  error.rs          Error (unified — see §4), ErrorClass, Sensitive<T>
118	  idempotency.rs    IdempotencyKey, already_done(), PartialSuccess
119	  recovery.rs       RecoveryHint, render_recovery()
120	  status.rs         StatusItem, StatusResponse, Health
121	  response.rs       AgentResponse builder, OutputFormat
122	
123	  resilience/
124	    mod.rs          RetryConfig, next_retry_delay(), parse_retry_after()  ← always
125	    policy.rs       with_resilience()                                      ← pipeline
126	    circuit.rs      CircuitBreaker, CircuitState                          ← pipeline
127	
128	  pipeline/
129	    mod.rs          Pipeline (pure data type + render())                   ← always
130	    executor.rs     PipelineExecutor, PipelineContext                     ← pipeline
131	    step.rs         Step, StepFn, StepContext, SkipReason                 ← pipeline
132	    graph.rs        assign_levels(), cycle detection                      ← pipeline
133	    result.rs       PipelineResult, RunStatus                             ← pipeline
134	    checkpoint.rs   Checkpoint, CheckpointStore, NoopCheckpointStore      ← pipeline
135	
136	  sink/
137	    mod.rs          OutputSink, AgentEvent, NoopSink                      ← pipeline
138	
139	  telemetry/
140	    mod.rs          TelemetryProvider, NoopProvider                       ← always (zero-cost)
141	
142	  ── Optional features ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
143	
144	  fuzzy/
145	    mod.rs          FuzzyMatcher, FuzzyResolver, Resolution<T>            ← fuzzy
146	    matcher.rs      nucleo-matcher wrapper, MatcherConfig                 ← fuzzy
147	    resolver.rs     Disambiguator trait, resolve()                        ← fuzzy
148	
149	  cache/
150	    mod.rs          Cache, CachePolicy, CacheEntry                        ← cache
151	    memory.rs       moka::future::Cache wrapper                           ← cache
152	    disk.rs         DiskCache, tag invalidation                           ← cache
153	    policy.rs       CachePolicyBuilder, stale-while-revalidate            ← cache
154	
155	  adapters/
156	    cli/
157	      mod.rs        CliSink, HumanWriter, JsonWriter                      ← cli
158	      checkpoint.rs DiskCheckpointStore                                   ← cli
159	      disambig.rs   TtyDisambiguator                                      ← cli
160	      ctrl_c.rs     install_ctrl_c_handler()                              ← cli
161	    mcp/
162	      mod.rs        McpSink                                               ← mcp
163	      checkpoint.rs MemoryCheckpointStore                                 ← mcp
164	      disambig.rs   McpDisambiguator                                      ← mcp
165	
166	  napi.rs           #[napi] exports                                       ← napi
167	```
168	
169	### Module principles
170	
171	- Pure vs async split within a module: sync computation always compiled, async
172	  extension behind `pipeline`. Pattern from `resilience/`: `next_retry_delay()`
173	  is always there; `with_resilience()` requires the feature.
174	- `pipeline::Pipeline` (pure data type + `render()`) is always compiled because
175	  tools may want to render a pipeline state without executing it.
176	- `telemetry` uses `NoopProvider` (zero-cost impl) so it compiles clean without
177	  a runtime dep.
178	
179	---
180	
181	## 4. Error type consolidation
182	
183	The original spec had `AxiError` (rendering-focused, michi) as a separate concept
184	from `AgentError` (infrastructure, the proposed execution spec). In a unified
185	crate these merge into `michi::Error`.
186	
187	```rust
188	// src/error.rs
189	#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
190	pub enum Error {
191	    // ── Execution errors (pipeline feature) ───────────────────────────────
192	    #[error("HTTP {status}: {message}")]
193	    Http { status: u16, message: String, retryable: bool, retry_after: Option<Duration> },
194	
195	    #[error("Timeout after {elapsed:?}")]
196	    Timeout { elapsed: Duration },
197	
198	    #[error("Step {id} failed")]
199	    StepFailed { id: String, #[source] source: Box<Error> },
200	
201	    #[error("Circuit {name} is open, retry after {retry_after:?}")]
202	    CircuitOpen { name: String, retry_after: Duration },
203	
204	    #[error("No match for query: {query}")]
205	    NoMatch { query: String },
206	
207	    #[error("Ambiguous match for {query}: {count} candidates")]
208	    AmbiguousMatch { query: String, count: usize },
209	
210	    #[error("Cyclic dependency: {cycle:?}")]
211	    CyclicDependency { cycle: Vec<String> },
212	
213	    #[error("Cancelled")]
214	    Cancelled,
215	
216	    #[error("Cache error: {0}")]
217	    Cache(String),
218	
219	    #[error(transparent)]
220	    Io(#[from] std::io::Error),
221	
222	    // ── Domain errors (always) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
223	    #[error("Invalid input: {0}")]
224	    InvalidInput(String),
225	
226	    #[error("Not found: {0}")]
227	    NotFound(String),
228	}
229	
230	impl Error {
231	    /// Render to agent-readable stdout string (AxiError-style).
232	    pub fn render(&self) -> String { ... }
233	    pub fn exit_code(&self) -> i32 { 1 }
234	    pub fn class(&self) -> ErrorClass { ... }
235	    pub fn is_retryable(&self) -> bool { ... }
236	}
237	
238	pub enum ErrorClass { User, Internal, Transient }
239	
240	/// Wrapper that omits the inner value from Debug/Display output.
241	pub struct Sensitive<T>(pub T);
242	```
243	
244	`Sensitive<T>` and `ErrorClass` are always compiled. The execution error variants
245	(`Http`, `Timeout`, `StepFailed`, `CircuitOpen`, `NoMatch`, `AmbiguousMatch`,
246	`CyclicDependency`, `Cancelled`, `Cache`) are gated behind `#[cfg(feature = "pipeline")]`.
247	
248	---
249	
250	## 5. Repo shape
251	
252	```
253	michi/                          ← git root: git@github.com:orin-axi/michi.git
254	  Cargo.toml                    ← [workspace] members + [package] michi lib
255	  Cargo.lock
256	  rust-toolchain.toml           ← pinned stable channel
257	  build.rs                      ← napi-build (conditional on napi feature)
258	  justfile                      ← unified task runner (see §6)
259	  .rustfmt.toml                 ← edition=2021, max_width=120
260	  .clippy.toml                  ← msrv, too-many-arguments-threshold=6
261	  .typos.toml                   ← spell-check config
262	  deny.toml                     ← license + advisory + bans policy
263	  CLAUDE.md                     ← agent session instructions
264	  README.md
265	  src/                          ← michi lib source (as above)
266	  benches/
267	    toon_render.rs
268	    kv_render.rs
269	    pipeline_render.rs
270	  tests/
271	    toon_integration.rs
272	    kv_integration.rs
273	    resilience_integration.rs

content.text: I've spot-verified several of the highest-severity claims directly (ran `cargo deny check`, `cargo tree`, grepped for serde usage, confirmed the spec text and the missing `#[must_use]` attributes myself) — they all hold up. I also merged two pairs of duplicate findings that separate dimensions independently discovered (the `escape_value` newline bug and the retry-jitter cap bug), which is a good sign of the review's internal consistency. Here's the final report.

findings.summary: escape_value() embeds raw newline/CR bytes inside quoted TOON values instead of truncating them, directly violating the crate's own spec.
findings.failure_scenario:
docs/01-spec.md:305-312 states as the authoritative grammar: "Values containing newlines MUST be truncated before rendering — TOON does not support multi-line cell values." escape_value() instead quotes them like a comma: `Value::Str("line one
line two")` renders as `"line one
line two"` with the raw 
 preserved verbatim inside the quotes. The output's physical line count then no longer matches the `type_name[N]{...}` row-count header, so any consumer reading exactly N lines after the header (the natural line-oriented reading this compact format invites) misattributes the continuation as a new/malformed row. tests/toon_integration.rs's `newline_in_value_is_quoted` locks in this spec-contradicting behavior as "expected," and truncate()/truncate_inline() only bound char count — neither strips embedded 
/, so nothing else in the crate enforces the spec's requirement. Independently found and confirmed by both the rust-practices and security review passes; I separately confirmed the docs/01-spec.md text and traced the call path myself.

findings.summary: next_retry_delay() adds jitter after capping at max_delay, so the returned delay can reach up to 2x max_delay — contradicting both its own field doc and function doc.
findings.failure_scenario: `capped_ms = raw_ms.min(max_delay_ms)` correctly bounds the base delay, but `jitter_ms = capped_ms * jitter_factor * jitter_seed` is then computed from the already-capped value and added on top (`capped_ms + jitter_ms`) rather than folded inside the cap. With `RetryConfig{max_delay: 30s, jitter_factor: 1.0}` (a documented legal 'full jitter' value) and `jitter_seed = 1.0` (the documented upper bound), the returned Duration is 60s — double the configured 30s ceiling. Even the crate's own default `jitter_factor: 0.2` produces up to 36s (20% over) once `raw_ms` reaches the cap. This directly contradicts `max_delay`'s doc comment ("Maximum delay cap — back-off never exceeds this") and `next_retry_delay`'s own doc ("capped at max_delay, with optional jitter"). The `#[allow(clippy::cast_possible_truncation, ...)]` above the function justifies its casts by claiming delays stay "≤ 30s by default," which this bug itself falsifies. Test coverage only exercises jitter_factor: 0.0 for the cap-related test, hiding the interaction. Independently found and confirmed by both the rust-practices and security review passes; I independently re-derived the same bound before the review ran.

findings.summary: AgentResponse::render_json's hand-rolled JSON string escaper only handles 5 characters, producing invalid JSON for other control bytes, and its justifying comment ("no serde dep in default features") is false — serde_json is already an unconditional dependency.
findings.failure_scenario: json_string() (lines 144-157) escapes only `"`, `\`, `\n`, `\r`, `\t` and passes every other byte through verbatim. `AgentResponse::new("hello\u{7}world").render(OutputFormat::Json)` embeds the raw 0x07 (BEL) byte inside the `"body":"..."` string; feeding that output into `serde_json::from_str` or a JS `JSON.parse()` fails, since RFC 8259 requires all U+0000–U+001F control characters to be escaped. Separately, `Cargo.toml` already lists `serde_json` as a non-optional dependency (confirmed via `cargo tree -p michi --no-default-features`), so the comment's premise for hand-rolling is currently false — michi could call `serde_json::Value`/`to_string` directly instead of a partially-correct hand-rolled escaper.

findings.summary: Pipeline::render() never escapes step.id and only partially escapes step.name (comma-check only, no quote-escaping), corrupting rows for realistic step names/ids — despite a correct, reusable escaper already existing one module away.
findings.failure_scenario: `PipelineStep{id: "s,extra".into(), name: "ok".into(), status: Completed}` renders the row `  s,extra,ok,completed` against the declared 3-column header `id,name,status` — 4 comma-separated fields for a 3-field schema, silently misaligning every subsequent column for a consumer that splits on commas per the declared header. Even when `step.name` does get quote-wrapped (line 78, gated only on `.contains(',')`), embedded `"` characters inside it are never escaped — unlike `toon::escape::escape_value`, which this module doesn't call — so a name like `he said "hi, there"` produces a malformed quoted field. The fix is straightforward: reuse `toon::escape::escape_value` here instead of hand-rolling a second, incomplete escaper.

findings.summary: deny.toml's `[licenses] deny = ["AGPL-3.0-or-later"]` key was removed from cargo-deny's config schema; `cargo deny check` fails immediately with a validation error before checking any dependency, so the AGPL-dependency ban currently provides zero protection.
findings.failure_scenario: Reproduced directly: `cargo deny check licenses` with the installed cargo-deny 0.19.9 errors `this key has been removed, see https://github.com/EmbarkStudios/cargo-deny/pull/611 ... failed to validate configuration file deny.toml` and exits without evaluating a single dependency's license. CI's `deny` job (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) uses `EmbarkStudios/cargo-deny-action@v2` with no pinned cargo-deny version, so it hits the same schema error — meaning `just check` and CI's Deny job are either failing closed right now (blocking all merges) or, if some other config path masks it, silently never enforcing the license ban this file exists for. The dependency-license discipline CLAUDE.md and deny.toml describe is not actually running.

findings.summary: serde and serde_json are unconditional (non-optional) dependencies of the default-feature build, directly contradicting the crate's "zero runtime deps by default" claim, and are entirely unused in src/.
findings.failure_scenario: Confirmed via `cargo tree -p michi --no-default-features`: it pulls in serde (with derive, i.e. serde_derive + syn + quote + proc-macro2 + unicode-ident), serde_core, and serde_json (itoa, memchr, zmij) — 11 extra crates compiled into every default-feature consumer (Monokl, Firkin, Lumen, Pulse, or any Rust CLI per the design doc's own consumer table: "Pure rendering (Rust CLI, no pipeline) → michi (defaults)"). `grep -rn 'serde\|Serialize\|Deserialize' src/` returns exactly one hit — a comment in response.rs claiming serde is absent. The stated architectural guarantee ("a consumer who adds michi with default features pulls in zero tokio, zero moka, zero nucleo" — and by extension, zero serde) is not actually true; serde/serde_json should be marked `optional = true` and gated behind whichever feature needs them, or removed if genuinely unused.

findings.summary: render_json always allocates a fixed 128-byte buffer regardless of actual content size, unlike render_text on the same struct, which sizes capacity from real content length.
findings.failure_scenario: `AgentResponse::new(body).render(OutputFormat::Json)` where `body` is a rendered TOON block for ~2,000 rows (~150-200KB, within michi's own stated "tens to low thousands of rows" target). `render_json()` starts at `String::with_capacity(128)` irrespective of `self.body.len()`; as `json_string` copies the ~200KB body character-by-character, the buffer must grow through roughly 11 successive reallocations (128→256→...→~262144), each copying everything accumulated so far (~400KB of redundant memmove total). `render_text` on the identical struct correctly computes `capacity = self.body.len() + hint_block.len() + recovery_block.len()` a few lines above — the JSON path just needs the same treatment.

findings.summary: The crate-wide #[allow(clippy::return_self_not_must_use)] is justified by a comment claiming "#[must_use] applied where appropriate," but none of the actual builder-chain methods carry it.
findings.failure_scenario: Removing the allow and rerunning `cargo clippy --all-features` produces exactly 6 "missing #[must_use] attribute on a method returning Self" warnings: `AgentResponse::with_hint/with_hints/with_recovery/with_recoveries/as_error` (src/response.rs:55,61,67,73,79) and `StatusResponse::with_hints` (src/status.rs:74) — confirmed by grepping response.rs/status.rs myself; none of these carry `#[must_use]` (only the terminal `render()`/`label()` methods do). Because `AgentResponse` derives `Clone`, this is a real footgun, not theoretical: `let r = AgentResponse::error(msg); if retry { r.clone().with_recovery(hint); }` silently drops the built response with no compiler warning, since the allow suppresses the exact lint that would catch it. Either add `#[must_use]` to the six methods or drop the justification comment, which currently misdescribes the codebase.

findings.summary: StepFailed's class()/is_retryable() ignore the wrapped source error's own classification, so a StepFailed wrapping a Transient (retryable) cause is itself always reported non-retryable.
findings.failure_scenario: `Error::StepFailed{id: "fetch".into(), source: Box::new(Error::Http{status: 503, message: "busy".into(), retryable: true, retry_after: None})}.is_retryable()` returns `false`, even though the inner `Http{retryable: true, ..}` alone reports `class() == Transient`. Confirmed by reading class()'s match arms (src/error.rs ~157-170): `StepFailed { .. }` is unconditionally grouped into the `Internal` arm regardless of what `source` is. `StepFailed` is the natural wrapper a Plan-2 pipeline step uses to attach step-id context to any underlying failure — any retry-orchestration code that checks only the outer error's `is_retryable()` (the documented, intended API) will silently stop retrying a transient failure the moment it gets wrapped with step context.

findings.summary: The root crate's `napi` feature is dead: nothing in src/ is gated behind cfg(feature = "napi"), and its sole real consumer, packages/michi-node, never enables it.
findings.failure_scenario: packages/michi-node/Cargo.toml depends on `michi = { path = "../.." }` with no `features = [...]` at all — confirmed by reading the file directly. The NAPI shim in packages/michi-node/src/lib.rs is written entirely against michi's plain always-compiled API and never touches anything the `napi` feature would add (there is no `src/napi.rs` implementing `#[napi]` exports inside the michi crate itself, despite the design doc's module map listing one). The crate doc comment (src/lib.rs) and the design doc both describe `napi` as "used by packages/michi-node," but that's not what's actually wired up — either the feature is vestigial and should be removed, or the intended napi.rs module was never built and the feature currently gates nothing.

findings.summary: Value::Int and Value::Float cells allocate a fresh heap String via n.to_string()/f.to_string() instead of writing directly into the pre-sized output buffer; the same pattern repeats in kv/mod.rs and pipeline/mod.rs.
findings.failure_scenario: Rendering a 2,000-row list with 2 numeric fields per row triggers 4,000 separate heap allocations via `n.to_string()`/`f.to_string()`, each immediately copied into `out` via push_str and dropped — work that `write!(out, "{n}")` via `std::fmt::Write` would do with zero extra allocations directly into the buffer `render()` already pre-sizes at the top of the function. The identical pattern recurs at src/kv/mod.rs (KvValue::Int/Float) and src/pipeline/mod.rs (step count formatting), so fixing it once as a shared helper would compound the benefit across every rendering hot path in the crate.

findings.summary: JsToonOptions places no bound on rows.len(), per-row field count, or hints.len(); a single NAPI call from untrusted JS can force unbounded synchronous allocation and O(rows×fields) work on Node's single-threaded event loop.
findings.failure_scenario: A JS caller (an MCP client, or a buggy/malicious tool invocation) calls render_toon with millions of row sub-arrays and/or very long strVal strings. render_toon eagerly maps every JsToonValue and calls michi::toon::render_toon, which pre-allocates a String sized by row_count*(field_count*12+10) and then writes every cell with no cap anywhere on the path. The call blocks the Node event loop for its full duration (starving all other in-flight requests on that process), and because Rust's default allocator aborts the whole process on OOM rather than panicking, #[napi(catch_unwind)] — which only catches Rust panics — provides no protection against this class of input. This is a real DoS surface specifically because the NAPI boundary is explicitly a trust boundary (untrusted JS crossing into Rust), unlike the rest of the crate where callers are same-process Rust code.

findings.summary: Duration::as_millis() returns u128; the `as u64` casts silently truncate (wrap, not saturate) for large-but-valid Duration values a caller can set on RetryConfig's unclamped base_delay/max_delay fields, contradicting the comment that claims the casts are safe.
findings.failure_scenario: `RetryConfig{ max_delay: Duration::from_secs(18_446_744_073_709_552), .. }` is a perfectly valid Duration (~584 million years, well inside Duration's u64-seconds range). `config.max_delay.as_millis()` = 18_446_744_073_709_552_000 (u128); the `as u64` cast wraps modulo 2^64 to exactly 384. next_retry_delay then silently treats the caller's ~584-million-year cap as a 384-millisecond cap. The line-47/48 comment claims the casts are "safe" because delays stay "≤ 30s by default" — true only for the untouched Default::default() config, not enforced for any config a caller actually constructs. Low practical likelihood (requires a deliberately extreme Duration), but the safety argument in the comment doesn't hold in general.

findings.summary: The pipeline feature enables tokio with features = ["full"], an anti-pattern for a library crate that forces every downstream pipeline/fuzzy/cache/cli/mcp consumer to compile all of tokio regardless of what Plan 2's step-orchestration executor actually needs.
findings.failure_scenario: tokio's own guidance is that `full` is meant for applications choosing every subsystem, not for libraries embedded by other crates — it forces the entire dependency/feature graph onto every downstream consumer regardless of use. Every one of Monokl, Firkin, Lumen, and Pulse that enables `pipeline` (directly, or transitively via fuzzy/cache/cli/mcp, all of which imply it) will unconditionally compile tokio's process-spawning, network I/O, signal-handling, and filesystem modules even though michi's own Plan 2 executor (per the design doc) is pure step-orchestration. Scoping to the specific tokio features actually needed (rt, macros, time, sync) would shrink build times and the dependency surface for every suite consumer.

findings.summary: The cli feature's dependency list omits atty, which the design doc explicitly lists as part of that feature ("Adds: indicatif, inquire, crossterm, ctrlc, atty"), and atty appears nowhere in Cargo.toml or Cargo.lock.
findings.failure_scenario: Confirmed by reading Cargo.toml directly: `cli = ["dep:indicatif", "dep:inquire", "dep:crossterm", "dep:ctrlc", "pipeline"]` — no atty. The design doc's header states "Implementation plans should treat this doc as authoritative" on topics it covers, including the feature taxonomy. A contributor implementing the Plan-2 adapters/cli/TtyDisambiguator per the design doc would expect atty to already be wired up; it isn't, so they'd either add it (reintroducing a crate with a known unsoundness advisory, RUSTSEC-2021-0145) or use std::io::IsTerminal instead, leaving the doc stale either way. Low severity since it only affects not-yet-built Plan 2 code, but worth reconciling now while the drift is small.

findings.summary: escape_value performs up to four separate full linear scans to decide whether escaping is needed, and over-allocates by up to 2x for the common comma-only-escape case, since the capacity guess assumes every character doubles when only embedded quotes do.
findings.failure_scenario: For a long string field (a multi-KB error message or log excerpt) whose only escape-triggering character is a newline near the end, `contains(',')` scans the full value, then `contains('"')` scans it again, before `contains('\n')` finally hits — 3 full passes before escaping even starts. Separately, a common real-world trigger like a location field `"San Francisco, CA"` (comma, no quotes) allocates `String::with_capacity(v.len()*2+2)` but only ever needs `v.len()+2` bytes (two surrounding quote chars) — a needless ~2x over-allocation on every comma-only value, which is the most common escaping case in practice.

findings.summary: render_text builds hint_block and recovery_block as fully separate owned Strings purely to measure their length for the final buffer's capacity, then copies both into a third buffer, doubling the allocation/copy cost of the hints+recovery portion on every call.
findings.failure_scenario: Every AgentResponse::render(OutputFormat::Text) call with any hints or recovery entries — the default, most common response path in the crate — allocates render_hints's own buffer, then render_recovery's own buffer, then a third `out` buffer sized from their combined length, then push_str-copies both prior buffers into it. For a response with 10 combined hint/recovery entries at ~60 bytes each, that's 2 extra heap allocations plus a redundant ~600-byte copy on every call that could instead push directly into `out`.

findings.summary: truncate() unconditionally performs a full content.chars().count() UTF-8 decode over the entire input before deciding whether truncation is needed, with no cheap byte-length short-circuit for the common already-within-budget case.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling truncate() on a large captured tool-output field (e.g. a 500KB stdout capture) with max_chars=200 — squarely the module's stated purpose — pays a full ~500,000-character UTF-8 decode via chars().count() merely to determine truncation is needed, before the actual bounded work happens. A `content.len() <= max_chars` guard at the top (valid since char count ≤ byte length for UTF-8) would let the common case of already-short content skip the scan entirely in O(1) instead of O(n).

findings.summary: No #![forbid(unsafe_code)] or #![deny(unsafe_code)] exists anywhere; the "no unsafe outside the napi boundary" non-negotiable is currently satisfied only because nobody has written unsafe yet, not by any mechanical enforcement.
findings.failure_scenario: Confirmed by grep: zero `unsafe` blocks exist in src/ or packages/michi-node/src/ today. But a future PR adding a performance optimization to src/toon/render.rs (e.g. an unsafe UTF-8 fast path) would compile cleanly with no error, since src/lib.rs has no `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` and nothing in CI (clippy config, deny.toml, lint attributes) would catch it at review or build time — the rule exists only as a line in CLAUDE.md, never mechanically checked. A one-line `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` on the lib crate (and a matching allow on the napi crate's boundary file if truly needed later) would close this for free.

findings.summary: IdempotencyKey is a newtype with Debug/Clone/PartialEq/Eq/Hash derives and two From impls, but the one function in its own module that conceptually needs a key, already_done(), never accepts an IdempotencyKey at all — it takes a raw Option<String>.
findings.failure_scenario: `grep -rn IdempotencyKey src/ tests/` shows the type is only constructed and compared inside idempotency.rs's own unit tests — never passed to already_done(stored: Option<String>), never stored in any map (no HashMap/BTreeMap exists anywhere in src/), and never referenced from response.rs, error.rs, or anywhere else. A downstream consumer building IdempotencyKey::new(hash_of_inputs) gets no compile-time connection between that key and the already_done() check — nothing in michi enforces that the string passed to already_done actually corresponds to a well-formed IdempotencyKey. Either wire already_done to accept &IdempotencyKey, or defer introducing the newtype until a Plan-2 consumer actually needs the type safety.

findings.summary: The "BTreeMap for output maps, HashMap for internal state only" non-negotiable currently has zero surface area to apply to — no module in src/ or packages/michi-node/src/ constructs a BTreeMap or HashMap of any kind.
findings.failure_scenario: `grep -rn 'BTreeMap\|HashMap' src/ packages/michi-node/src/` returns no matches. Not a violation today (there is no HashMap being used where a BTreeMap should be) — this is an observation, not a defect: the rule is aspirational for whichever future module first needs an ordered output map. Worth keeping in mind so the first PR that introduces one doesn't reach for HashMap by habit, since nothing currently enforces the distinction.

The adversarial review is complete: 98 agents (5 dimension finders + up to 3 verification lenses per candidate finding) surfaced 31 candidate defects, 23 survived verification, and I merged 2 duplicate pairs independently caught by both the rust-practices and security passes — 21 findings reported above, ranked most-severe first.

**Highlights, in order of what actually matters:**

- **Critical:** `escape_value()` (src/toon/escape.rs:10) embeds raw `\n`/`\r` bytes inside quoted TOON output instead of truncating them — this directly contradicts the crate's own spec (`docs/01-spec.md`), which mandates newlines "MUST be truncated before rendering." I confirmed the spec text and the code path myself.
- **High, and empirically confirmed by me directly:**
  - `next_retry_delay()` adds jitter *after* capping at `max_delay`, so a retry delay can reach 2x the configured ceiling — contradicts its own doc comment.
  - `cargo deny check` **fails outright** on this repo's `deny.toml` (I reproduced the exact schema error) — the AGPL dependency ban is currently not running at all, in CI or locally.
  - `serde`/`serde_json` are unconditional dependencies of the default build (confirmed via `cargo tree --no-default-features`) despite the crate's "zero deps by default" claim, and grep shows they're unused in `src/`.
  - `render_json`'s hand-rolled escaper produces invalid JSON for control characters; `Pipeline::render()` has its own separate, broken escaping that doesn't reuse the correct `toon::escape_value`; and the `#[must_use]` builder-method gap I verified by grep.
- **Medium/Low:** a `StepFailed` error-classification bug that silently downgrades retryable errors, a dead `napi` feature, a real (if narrow) DoS surface at the NAPI boundary, plus several genuine allocation-pattern inefficiencies and doc/implementation drift items.

Two items (`IdempotencyKey` being unused, and the `BTreeMap` non-negotiable having no current surface area) are lower-confidence/observational rather than active bugs — marked PLAUSIBLE rather than CONFIRMED.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/gabe/.claude/plugins/cache/superpowers-marketplace/superpowers/5.1.0/skills/dispatching-parallel-agents

# Dispatching Parallel Agents

## Overview

You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

When you have multiple unrelated failures (different test files, different subsystems, different bugs), investigating them sequentially wastes time. Each investigation is independent and can happen in parallel.

**Core principle:** Dispatch one agent per independent problem domain. Let them work concurrently.

## When to Use

```dot
digraph when_to_use {
    "Multiple failures?" [shape=diamond];
    "Are they independent?" [shape=diamond];
    "Single agent investigates all" [shape=box];
    "One agent per problem domain" [shape=box];
    "Can they work in parallel?" [shape=diamond];
    "Sequential agents" [shape=box];
    "Parallel dispatch" [shape=box];

    "Multiple failures?" -> "Are they independent?" [label="yes"];
    "Are they independent?" -> "Single agent investigates all" [label="no - related"];
    "Are they independent?" -> "Can they work in parallel?" [label="yes"];
    "Can they work in parallel?" -> "Parallel dispatch" [label="yes"];
    "Can they work in parallel?" -> "Sequential agents" [label="no - shared state"];
}
```

**Use when:**
- 3+ test files failing with different root causes
- Multiple subsystems broken independently
- Each problem can be understood without context from others
- No shared state between investigations

**Don't use when:**
- Failures are related (fix one might fix others)
- Need to understand full system state
- Agents would interfere with each other

## The Pattern

### 1. Identify Independent Domains

Group failures by what's broken:
- File A tests: Tool approval flow
- File B tests: Batch completion behavior
- File C tests: Abort functionality

Each domain is independent - fixing tool approval doesn't affect abort tests.

### 2. Create Focused Agent Tasks

Each agent gets:
- **Specific scope:** One test file or subsystem
- **Clear goal:** Make these tests pass
- **Constraints:** Don't change other code
- **Expected output:** Summary of what you found and fixed

### 3. Dispatch in Parallel

```typescript
// In Claude Code / AI environment
Task("Fix agent-tool-abort.test.ts failures")
Task("Fix batch-completion-behavior.test.ts failures")
Task("Fix tool-approval-race-conditions.test.ts failures")
// All three run concurrently
```

### 4. Review and Integrate

When agents return:
- Read each summary
- Verify fixes don't conflict
- Run full test suite
- Integrate all changes

## Agent Prompt Structure

Good agent prompts are:
1. **Focused** - One clear problem domain
2. **Self-contained** - All context needed to understand the problem
3. **Specific about output** - What should the agent return?

```markdown
Fix the 3 failing tests in src/agents/agent-tool-abort.test.ts:

1. "should abort tool with partial output capture" - expects 'interrupted at' in message
2. "should handle mixed completed and aborted tools" - fast tool aborted instead of completed
3. "should properly track pendingToolCount" - expects 3 results but gets 0

These are timing/race condition issues. Your task:

1. Read the test file and understand what each test verifies
2. Identify root cause - timing issues or actual bugs?
3. Fix by:
   - Replacing arbitrary timeouts with event-based waiting
   - Fixing bugs in abort implementation if found
   - Adjusting test expectations if testing changed behavior

Do NOT just increase timeouts - find the real issue.

Return: Summary of what you found and what you fixed.
```

## Common Mistakes

**❌ Too broad:** "Fix all the tests" - agent gets lost
**✅ Specific:** "Fix agent-tool-abort.test.ts" - focused scope

**❌ No context:** "Fix the race condition" - agent doesn't know where
**✅ Context:** Paste the error messages and test names

**❌ No constraints:** Agent might refactor everything
**✅ Constraints:** "Do NOT change production code" or "Fix tests only"

**❌ Vague output:** "Fix it" - you don't know what changed
**✅ Specific:** "Return summary of root cause and changes"

## When NOT to Use

**Related failures:** Fixing one might fix others - investigate together first
**Need full context:** Understanding requires seeing entire system
**Exploratory debugging:** You don't know what's broken yet
**Shared state:** Agents would interfere (editing same files, using same resources)

## Real Example from Session

**Scenario:** 6 test failures across 3 files after major refactoring

**Failures:**
- agent-tool-abort.test.ts: 3 failures (timing issues)
- batch-completion-behavior.test.ts: 2 failures (tools not executing)
- tool-approval-race-conditions.test.ts: 1 failure (execution count = 0)

**Decision:** Independent domains - abort logic separate from batch completion separate from race conditions

**Dispatch:**
```
Agent 1 → Fix agent-tool-abort.test.ts
Agent 2 → Fix batch-completion-behavior.test.ts
Agent 3 → Fix tool-approval-race-conditions.test.ts
```

**Results:**
- Agent 1: Replaced timeouts with event-based waiting
- Agent 2: Fixed event structure bug (threadId in wrong place)
- Agent 3: Added wait for async tool execution to complete

**Integration:** All fixes independent, no conflicts, full suite green

**Time saved:** 3 problems solved in parallel vs sequentially

## Key Benefits

1. **Parallelization** - Multiple investigations happen simultaneously
2. **Focus** - Each agent has narrow scope, less context to track
3. **Independence** - Agents don't interfere with each other
4. **Speed** - 3 problems solved in time of 1

## Verification

After agents return:
1. **Review each summary** - Understand what changed
2. **Check for conflicts** - Did agents edit same code?
3. **Run full suite** - Verify all fixes work together
4. **Spot check** - Agents can make systematic errors

## Real-World Impact

From debugging session (2025-10-03):
- 6 failures across 3 files
- 3 agents dispatched in parallel
- All investigations completed concurrently
- All fixes integrated successfully
- Zero conflicts between agent changes

Good fit for this — dispatching-parallel-agents is exactly this shape (independent bugs, no shared state), not a full Workflow. Since ultracode is off, spinning up the heavy Workflow orchestrator would be overkill for ~1900 lines of already-diagnosed fixes anyway.

**My recommendation on process:** skip Workflow, use the plain Agent tool with one agent per independent file-cluster (not per finding — several findings share a file and would conflict if split across agents). Mapping the 21 findings to disjoint file ownership gives about 9 clusters:

| Cluster | Files | Findings |
|---|---|---|
| A | `toon/escape.rs`, `toon/render.rs` | critical newline bug, escape scan/capacity, numeric-cell alloc |
| B | `kv/mod.rs` | numeric-cell alloc (same pattern) |
| C | `pipeline/mod.rs` | escaping reuse, numeric-cell alloc |
| D | `resilience/mod.rs` | jitter/cap bug, u128→u64 truncation |
| E | `lib.rs`, `response.rs`, `status.rs` | JSON escaping, JSON/text buffer sizing, `must_use`, `forbid(unsafe_code)` |
| F | `error.rs` | StepFailed class propagation |
| H | `Cargo.toml`, `deny.toml`, `michi-node/Cargo.toml` | serde optional, napi feature, tokio `full`, atty, deny.toml schema |
| I | `packages/michi-node/src/lib.rs` | unbounded NAPI input |
| J | `truncate.rs` | byte-length short-circuit |

Each agent works in the main tree directly (no worktree needed — clusters don't overlap), follows TDD, and returns a diff summary; I review all of them together and run `just check && just test` once at the end to catch cross-cluster breakage before anything's considered done.

Two of these aren't mechanical, though — they need a call only you can make:

questions.question: escape_value() currently embeds raw newlines/CRs inside quoted TOON values, contradicting the spec's "MUST be truncated before rendering" rule. How should it actually handle them?

options.label: Strip \n/\r before quoting (Recommended)
options.description: Matches the spec's literal wording. Simplest, keeps render_toon infallible. Lossy — the newline content is gone from output, not just escaped.

options.label: JSON-style escape as literal \n / \r
options.description: Round-trippable (no data loss), but changes the escaping contract from "quote-doubling only" to a fuller backslash-escape scheme, and updates the spec doc instead of the code.

options.label: Reject with an error
options.description: render_toon (or escape_value) returns a Result and forces the caller to pre-sanitize. Matches "MUST be truncated before rendering" most literally, but breaks the current infallible API and touches every call site.

questions.question: michi's own `napi` feature (Cargo.toml) is currently vestigial — packages/michi-node depends on michi without enabling it, and there's no src/napi.rs implementing #[napi] exports inside the main crate, despite the design doc's module map listing one. What should happen to it?

options.label: Remove the unused feature/deps for now (Recommended)
options.description: YAGNI for the MVP: drop napi/napi-derive optional deps and the napi feature from the root Cargo.toml since nothing currently uses them. Design doc gets a note that this is deferred.

options.label: Build out src/napi.rs per the design doc
options.description: Move packages/michi-node's #[napi] export functions into a real src/napi.rs behind the napi feature, matching the original module-map design. More work, but closes the architecture gap instead of just removing the aspiration.

questions.question: Which findings should this round of fixes cover?

options.label: All 19 confirmed + review the 2 plausible ones (Recommended)
options.description: Full cleanup in one pass while the review context is fresh. The 2 PLAUSIBLE ones (unused IdempotencyKey, BTreeMap non-negotiable observation) get a quick look — may end up as "no action needed" rather than a code change.

options.label: Critical + High only (9 findings)
options.description: Fix the correctness/security-impacting bugs now; leave the Medium/Low performance and hygiene items as a tracked follow-up backlog for later.

input.description: Fix cluster A: toon escape+render
input.name: agent-A

Repo: /Users/gabe/Projects/michi (Rust crate "michi" — pure rendering primitives, no unwrap/expect/panic/unsafe in lib code, BTreeMap for output maps, String::with_capacity pre-allocation, char-boundary-safe truncation — see CLAUDE.md at repo root for the full non-negotiables list). This crate just went through an adversarial code review; you're fixing 3 confirmed findings, all scoped to src/toon/escape.rs and src/toon/render.rs only. Do NOT touch any other files.

Follow test-driven development: for each fix, first write or extend a test that fails against the current code and demonstrates the bug, confirm it fails, then implement the fix, then confirm the test passes.

FINDING 1 (critical, src/toon/escape.rs:10, escape_value): It currently embeds raw newline/CR bytes inside quoted values instead of stripping them, contradicting docs/01-spec.md's explicit rule: "Values containing newlines MUST be truncated before rendering — TOON does not support multi-line cell values." Decision made: strip embedded \n and \r characters from the value before/while quoting (do not JSON-escape them as literal \n, do not make the function fallible — just remove the newline/CR bytes so the physical-line-per-row invariant holds). Note there is an existing test `value_with_newline_is_quoted` and `value_with_cr_is_quoted` in src/toon/escape.rs's test module (and possibly a `newline_in_value_is_quoted` test in tests/toon_integration.rs) that currently assert the OLD (buggy) behavior — update those tests to assert the new stripped behavior instead of deleting them blind; read them first to understand exactly what they check.

FINDING 2 (low, src/toon/escape.rs:10, escape_value): The function does up to 4 separate full linear scans (`contains(',')`, `contains('"')`, `contains('\n')`, `contains('\r')`) before deciding whether to escape, and its capacity guess `v.len() * 2 + 2` over-allocates by ~2x for the common case (e.g. a value with a comma but no quotes only needs `v.len() + 2` bytes, not double). Fix: scan the value once (e.g. a single loop or single pass classification) to decide escaping and the correct capacity, rather than 4 separate `.contains()` calls, and size the buffer based on what's actually needed (only quote characters double).

FINDING 3 (medium, src/toon/render.rs:55, part of a repo-wide pattern — you only need to fix the toon/ instance): `Value::Int(n) => Cow::Owned(n.to_string())` and the `Value::Float` arm each allocate a fresh heap String per numeric cell instead of writing directly into the pre-sized `out` buffer that `render()` already allocates at the top of the function. Fix by using `std::fmt::Write` (`use std::fmt::Write as _;` then `write!(out, "{n}")` or similar) to format numbers directly into `out`, removing the per-cell Cow::Owned/to_string() allocation for the Int and Float arms specifically. Str/Bool/Null arms can stay as they are (Bool/Null don't allocate; Str needs escape_value's Cow). Watch out: the current code builds a `s` Cow value per iteration then does `out.push_str(&s)` — you'll need to restructure that small loop so the Int/Float cases write straight into `out` while Str/Bool/Null still work correctly for the same loop; make sure the comma-separator logic (`if i > 0 { out.push(','); }`) still works with the restructure.

When done, run `cargo fmt` on the touched files, then `cargo nextest run -p michi` and `cargo clippy -p michi --all-features -- -D warnings` and confirm both are clean. Return: a summary of the tests you added/changed and the fixes you made, plus the final test/clippy output confirming everything passes.

input.description: Fix cluster C: pipeline escaping
input.name: agent-C
input.prompt:
Repo: /Users/gabe/Projects/michi (Rust crate "michi" — pure rendering primitives; see CLAUDE.md at repo root for non-negotiables: no unwrap/expect/panic/unsafe in lib code, String::with_capacity pre-allocation, etc.). Tests run via `cargo nextest run` (not `cargo test`). You're fixing 2 confirmed findings from an adversarial code review, scoped to src/pipeline/mod.rs only. Do NOT touch any other files — in particular, do not touch src/toon/ files; a helper you need has already been exposed for you (see below).

Follow test-driven development: for each fix, first write or extend a test that fails against the current code and demonstrates the bug, confirm it fails, then implement the fix, then confirm the test passes.

FINDING 1 (high, src/pipeline/mod.rs, Pipeline::render(), around line 73-88): `step.id` is pushed via `out.push_str(&step.id)` with NO escaping at all, and `step.name` is only quote-wrapped `if step.name.contains(',')` with no internal quote-escaping even when wrapped — e.g. `PipelineStep{id: "s,extra", name: "ok", ..}` renders the row `  s,extra,ok,completed` against the declared 3-column header `id,name,status`, silently producing 4 comma-separated fields for a 3-field schema. And a name like `he said "hi, there"` would be quote-wrapped (contains a comma) but its embedded `"` characters are never escaped, producing a malformed quoted field.

Fix: reuse the crate's existing, correct escaper instead of hand-rolling a second one. It has just been exposed as `pub(crate) use escape::escape_value;` in src/toon/mod.rs, so from src/pipeline/mod.rs you can call `crate::toon::escape_value(&step.id)` and `crate::toon::escape_value(&step.name)` — each returns a `Cow<str>` that is already correctly comma/quote/newline-escaped and quoted only when needed. Replace both the raw `step.id` push and the manual `if step.name.contains(',')` quoting logic with calls to this shared escaper, matching how src/toon/render.rs already uses it for row values.

FINDING 2 (medium, src/pipeline/mod.rs, part of a repo-wide pattern found in numeric-cell rendering — you only need to fix the pipeline/ instance): the step-count line `out.push_str(&n.to_string())` (where `n = self.steps.len()`) allocates a heap String via `.to_string()` instead of writing directly into the pre-sized `out` buffer. Fix using `std::fmt::Write` (`use std::fmt::Write as _;` then something like `write!(out, "{n}")`, ignoring/handling the infallible Result without unwrap/expect per this crate's lint rules, e.g. `let _ = write!(out, "{n}");`).

Existing tests (`renders_pipeline_steps`, `step_name_with_comma_is_quoted`, etc.) check exact output strings — read them first; you may need to update their expected strings if the escaping behavior for the comma-containing case changes shape (e.g. previously unescaped `"Parse, validate"` may now be produced via the shared escaper, which should still quote-wrap it the same way, but double check exact output matches what escape_value actually produces).

input.description: Fix cluster D: resilience jitter+cast
input.name: agent-D
input.prompt:
Repo: /Users/gabe/Projects/michi (Rust crate "michi" — pure rendering primitives; see CLAUDE.md at repo root for non-negotiables: no unwrap/expect/panic/unsafe in lib code, etc.). Tests run via `cargo nextest run` (not `cargo test`). You're fixing 2 confirmed findings from an adversarial code review, scoped to src/resilience/mod.rs only. Do NOT touch any other files.

Follow test-driven development: for each fix, first write or extend a test that fails against the current code and demonstrates the bug, confirm it fails, then implement the fix, then confirm the test passes.

FINDING 1 (high, src/resilience/mod.rs, next_retry_delay(), around lines 50-60): the function computes `capped_ms = raw_ms.min(max_delay_ms)` (correctly bounding the base exponential-backoff delay), but then computes `jitter_ms = capped_ms as f64 * jitter_factor * jitter_seed` FROM THE ALREADY-CAPPED VALUE and returns `capped_ms + jitter_ms` — so the final result can exceed `max_delay` by up to `jitter_factor * 100%` (e.g. with the crate's own `jitter_factor: 0.2` default and an attempt where `raw_ms >= max_delay`, the returned Duration is up to 20% over the cap; with `jitter_factor: 1.0`, a documented legal value, it can be a full 2x the cap). This directly contradicts `RetryConfig::max_delay`'s doc comment ("Maximum delay cap — back-off never exceeds this") and `next_retry_delay`'s own doc comment ("capped at max_delay, with optional jitter").

Fix so `max_delay` is an actual hard ceiling that is never exceeded, while jitter still has a meaningful effect at low attempt counts (i.e. don't just tack `.min(max_delay_ms)` onto the very end in a way that makes jitter a no-op once `raw_ms` alone would already hit the cap — think about it as: apply jitter to the pre-cap `raw_ms` first — `raw_ms + jitter_ms` where `jitter_ms` is derived from `raw_ms` — and cap the jittered total once, at the end, against `max_delay`). Use your judgment on the exact formula as long as: (a) the returned Duration can never exceed `config.max_delay` for any legal `jitter_factor`/`jitter_seed` in `[0.0, 1.0]`, and (b) jitter still visibly varies the delay for attempts where the base exponential delay hasn't yet reached the cap. Update the doc comments if the exact jitter semantics change (e.g. "jitter is added to the pre-cap delay, then the result is capped"). The existing test `delay_is_capped_at_max` only exercises `jitter_factor: 0.0` and won't catch this — add a new test with a nonzero jitter_factor (e.g. 1.0) and an attempt/base_delay combination where the pre-jitter delay already reaches max_delay, asserting the result never exceeds max_delay. Also keep the existing `jitter_increases_delay` test passing (jitter should still make delay strictly increase relative to no-jitter, at least when not already capped).

FINDING 2 (medium, src/resilience/mod.rs, lines ~55/57): `config.base_delay.as_millis() as u64` and `config.max_delay.as_millis() as u64` — `Duration::as_millis()` returns `u128`, and the bare `as u64` cast silently wraps (not saturates) for extreme-but-valid Duration values a caller could construct (e.g. `Duration::from_secs(18_446_744_073_709_552)`, a valid ~584-million-year Duration, wraps to 384ms). The comment above the function claims the casts are "safe" because delays stay "≤ 30s by default" — true only for the untouched `Default::default()` config, not for any config a caller actually builds. Fix by replacing the bare `as u64` casts with a saturating conversion, e.g. `u64::try_from(config.base_delay.as_millis()).unwrap_or(u64::MAX)` (note: `unwrap_or` on a Result is fine here, it's not `.unwrap()`/`.expect()` on the Result itself, so it doesn't violate the crate's unwrap/expect ban — but double check by running clippy after; if `clippy::unwrap_used` still flags it, use `.map_or(u64::MAX, |v| v)` or `.ok().unwrap_or(u64::MAX)` — whatever passes clippy cleanly). Add a test constructing an extreme Duration and confirming the function no longer wraps to a tiny value (e.g. assert the resulting delay saturates to a very large value rather than wrapping small).

When done, run `cargo fmt` on src/resilience/mod.rs, then `cargo nextest run -p michi` and `cargo clippy -p michi --all-features -- -D warnings` and confirm both are clean. Return: a summary of the tests you added/changed, the exact fix formulas you used, and the final test/clippy output confirming everything passes.

input.description: Fix cluster E: lib/response/status
input.name: agent-E
input.prompt:
Repo: /Users/gabe/Projects/michi (Rust crate "michi" — pure rendering primitives; see CLAUDE.md at repo root for non-negotiables: no unwrap/expect/panic/unsafe in lib code, String::with_capacity pre-allocation, etc.). Tests run via `cargo nextest run` (not `cargo test`). You're fixing 5 confirmed findings from an adversarial code review, scoped to src/lib.rs, src/response.rs, and src/status.rs only. Do NOT touch any other files.

Follow test-driven development: for each fix, first write or extend a test that fails against the current code and demonstrates the bug, confirm it fails, then implement the fix, then confirm the test passes.

FINDING 1 (high, src/response.rs, json_string(), around lines 144-157): the hand-rolled JSON string escaper only escapes `"`, `\`, `\n`, `\r`, `\t` and passes every other byte through verbatim, producing invalid JSON for other control characters (RFC 8259 requires ALL U+0000–U+001F control characters to be escaped). E.g. `AgentResponse::new("hello\u{7}world").render(OutputFormat::Json)` embeds a raw BEL (0x07) byte inside the JSON string, which `serde_json::from_str` or a JS `JSON.parse()` would reject. Fix: extend the match in `json_string()` to escape any remaining char with codepoint < 0x20 as a `\u00XX` escape (uppercase or lowercase hex, either is valid JSON — be consistent), in addition to the existing named escapes. Do NOT introduce a serde_json dependency for this — keep it hand-rolled and dependency-free (a sibling fix elsewhere in this codebase is specifically making serde_json properly optional/unused in the default build, so pulling it in here would undo that). Add tests with a few different control characters (e.g. \u{0}, \u{1}, \u{7}, \u{1F}) confirming they're now escaped as `\u00XX` and that `\n`/`\r`/`\t`/`"`/`\\` still use their existing named short escapes (don't double-escape those).

FINDING 2 (high, src/response.rs, render_json(), around line 110): `String::with_capacity(128)` is a fixed constant regardless of `self.body.len()`, `self.hints`, or `self.recovery` sizes — for a large body (e.g. tens of KB), this causes many reallocations copying the whole buffer each time. Fix by sizing capacity from actual content, similar to how `render_text()` a few lines above already does it (`let capacity = self.body.len() + hint_block.len() + recovery_block.len();`) — a reasonable estimate for JSON is body length plus some overhead per hint/recovery entry plus a constant for the JSON punctuation, e.g. `self.body.len() + self.hints.iter().map(|h| h.as_str().len() + 16).sum::<usize>() + self.recovery.len() * 64 + 64`. Exact formula is your judgment; it just needs to avoid the fixed-128 constant and scale with real content size. Don't worry about exact byte-perfect sizing — a reasonable lower/upper bound that avoids repeated reallocation for realistic sizes is the goal.

FINDING 3 (low, src/response.rs, render_text(), around line 97-106): builds `hint_block` and `recovery_block` as fully separate owned Strings (via `render_hints()`/`render_recovery()`) purely to measure their `.len()` for the final buffer's capacity, then copies both into a third `out` buffer via `push_str`. This double-allocates+double-copies the hints/recovery portion on every call that has any hints or recovery entries. Use your judgment on how much to fix here: at minimum, if a full rework is too invasive, at least avoid a THIRD allocation by pushing directly into `out` instead of building `out` as a brand new buffer and copying hint_block/recovery_block into it (i.e., pre-size `out` using a capacity estimate that doesn't require having built hint_block/recovery_block first — e.g. `self.body.len() + self.hints.len() * 60 + self.recovery.len() * 80` — then push body, then call `crate::hints::append_hints(&mut out, &self.hints)` and an equivalent in-place append for recovery instead of calling the buffer-returning `render_hints`/`render_recovery`). FINDING 4 (high/lint-hygiene, src/lib.rs + src/response.rs + src/status.rs): src/lib.rs has `#![allow(clippy::return_self_not_must_use)]` justified by a comment claiming "#[must_use] applied where appropriate" — but none of `AgentResponse::with_hint`, `with_hints`, `with_recovery`, `with_recoveries`, `as_error` (src/response.rs) or `StatusResponse::with_hints` (src/status.rs) actually carry `#[must_use]`. Repo: /Users/gabe/Projects/michi (Rust crate "michi" — pure rendering primitives; see CLAUDE.md at repo root for non-negotiables: no unwrap/expect/panic/unsafe in lib code, etc.). Tests run via `cargo nextest run` (not `cargo test`). You're fixing one confirmed correctness bug from an adversarial code review, scoped to src/error.rs only. Do NOT touch any other files.

Follow test-driven development: first write a test that fails against the current code and demonstrates the bug, confirm it fails, then implement the fix, then confirm the test passes.

FINDING (medium, src/error.rs, Error::class(), around lines 156-170, feature = "pipeline"): `StepFailed { .. }` is unconditionally grouped into the `ErrorClass::Internal` match arm regardless of what its wrapped `source` error actually is. So `Error::StepFailed{id: "fetch".into(), source: Box::new(Error::Http{status: 503, message: "busy".into(), retryable: true, retry_after: None})}.is_retryable()` returns `false`, even though the inner `Http{retryable: true, ..}` on its own reports `class() == ErrorClass::Transient` / `is_retryable() == true`. Since `StepFailed` is the natural wrapper a pipeline step uses to attach step-id context to any underlying failure, wrapping silently downgrades a retryable cause to non-retryable for any caller that checks only the outer error.

Fix: change the `Self::StepFailed { .. }` arm in `class()` to delegate to the wrapped source's own classification instead of hardcoding `Internal` — e.g. `Self::StepFailed { source, .. } => source.class()`. This requires `class()` to recurse into `source.class()` (source is `Box<Self>`, so this is a straightforward recursive call — no unsafe/unwrap needed, just a method call through the Box). Note this code is behind `#[cfg(feature = "pipeline")]`, so you'll need `cargo nextest run -p michi --features pipeline` (not just the default feature set) to actually exercise it. Add a test (behind the same `#[cfg(feature = "pipeline")]` gate as the existing pipeline-only tests, if any exist in this file, or add the cfg gate yourself if the test module isn't already gated) constructing a `StepFailed` wrapping a `Transient`-classified error (e.g. `Http{retryable: true, ..}` or `Timeout{..}`) and asserting `.is_retryable() == true`, and another wrapping a `User`-classified error (e.g. this crate's `InvalidInput`) if that's a plausible source type, confirming it correctly propagates as non-retryable too — pick realistic source variants that exist in this enum.

When done, run `cargo fmt` on src/error.rs, then `cargo nextest run -p michi --features pipeline` and `cargo clippy -p michi --features pipeline -- -D warnings` and confirm both are clean.
