Repo: /Users/gabe/Projects/michi (Rust crate "michi" — pure rendering primitives; see CLAUDE.md at repo root for non-negotiables, especially: truncation MUST use char boundaries, never byte-slice blindly). Tests run via `cargo nextest run` (not `cargo test`). You're fixing one confirmed performance finding from an adversarial code review, scoped to src/truncate.rs only. Do NOT touch any other files.

Follow test-driven development: first write or extend a test that demonstrates the current behavior is preserved (correctness must not regress — this fix is purely a perf short-circuit, not a behavior change), then implement, then confirm all tests pass.

FINDING (low, src/truncate.rs, truncate(), around line 20): the function unconditionally computes `let char_count = content.chars().count();` — a full UTF-8 decode over the ENTIRE input — before checking `if char_count <= max_chars`. For already-short content (the common case for most calls, e.g. a short status field that happens to be well within budget) called with a very large `content` (e.g. a 500KB captured stdout buffer) and a `max_chars` the content already satisfies, this pays the full O(n) scan unconditionally.

Fix: add a cheap byte-length fast path before the expensive char count. Since for valid UTF-8, `char count <= byte length` always holds, `content.len() <= max_chars` guarantees `content.chars().count() <= max_chars` is also true (byte length is an upper bound on char count) — so if `content.len() <= max_chars`, you can skip the `chars().count()` scan entirely and return `Truncated { content: content.to_string(), original_len: content.len(), was_truncated: false }` immediately, exactly like the existing early-return path. Be careful: this short-circuit is a *sufficient* condition (if byte len is within budget, char count definitely is too), but NOT computing char_count in that branch means you must NOT need char_count for anything else in that early-return path — check the function body to confirm `original_len` uses `content.len()` (byte length), not `char_count`, in the existing early return (it does, per the current code — `original_len: content.len()`), so this should be a safe, transparent optimization. The full `chars().count()` path is still needed when `content.len() > max_chars` (byte length exceeding max_chars doesn't tell you char count relationship, since multi-byte chars mean char count could still be <= max_chars).

Add a test with a large-but-short-in-chars string (e.g. a few thousand ASCII bytes, well under some generous max_chars) confirming `was_truncated == false` and the content is returned unchanged, to lock in the fast path's correctness. Keep all existing tests (`short_content_not_truncated`, `long_content_is_truncated`, `truncation_respects_char_boundaries`, `truncate_inline_returns_string`, `exact_length_not_truncated`, `suffix_contains_original_char_count`) passing exactly as before — this must not change any observable behavior, only skip unnecessary work in the short-content case.

When done, run `cargo fmt` on src/truncate.rs, then `cargo nextest run -p michi` and `cargo clippy -p michi --all-features -- -D warnings` and confirm both are clean. Return: a summary of the fix and the final test/clippy output confirming everything passes.

content.text:
All 21 findings from the review are now fixed and verified. Summary:

**Approach:** 8 parallel agents (one per disjoint file cluster, via `dispatching-parallel-agents`, not the heavyweight Workflow tool) + me handling the riskiest piece directly (the `napi` feature rebuild, since it had real runtime/linking risk).

**What landed:**
- `escape_value` now strips embedded `\n`/`\r` (per your call), fixed in one pass, one linear scan, correct capacity
- `next_retry_delay` jitter now applied pre-cap so `max_delay` is a true ceiling; `Duration` casts saturate instead of wrapping
- `render_json` now escapes all JSON control chars and sizes its buffer from actual content; `render_text` appends in-place instead of double-buffering
- All 6 builder methods got `#[must_use]`; the now-unjustified clippy allow was removed
- `Pipeline::render()` reuses the crate's real escaper instead of a second broken one
- `StepFailed` now delegates classification to its wrapped source
- `serde`/`serde_json` removed (were unused), `tokio` scoped down from `full`, `deny.toml` migrated to the current cargo-deny schema, doc drift on `atty` resolved in favor of `std::io::IsTerminal`
- Numeric-cell rendering across toon/kv/pipeline now writes into the buffer instead of allocating per cell

content.text:
Good news first: I ran `cargo publish --dry-run -p michi` and it packages and verifies cleanly — the Rust side of the crate itself is technically publishable today. But there are real gaps before you'd want to actually do it, plus one concrete security gap in CI I found while checking. Here's the full picture.

## Publish readiness

**crates.io (`michi`)** — mostly ready
- ✅ `Cargo.toml` has name/version/description/license/repository/keywords/categories; `cargo publish --dry-run` succeeds clean
- ❌ No `README.md`, and no `readme` field in `Cargo.toml` — the crates.io page will be blank
- ❌ No `LICENSE` file in the repo — you should ship the actual AGPL-3.0 text, both for compliance and because crates.io/GitHub both look for it
- ⚠️ `rust-toolchain.toml` pins the floating `stable` channel, not a specific version — the design doc calls for "pinned stable channel" but this isn't actually pinned, so builds aren't fully reproducible over time
- ⚠️ Worth checking now, before you're committed to it: is the name `michi` still available on crates.io?

**npm (`packages/michi-node`)** — has real gaps
- ✅ `package.json` has the right metadata; local build+test verified end-to-end this session
- ❌ No `napi` config in `package.json`/`Cargo.toml` for cross-platform publishing — `napi prepublish -t npm` needs to know the target triples to generate the per-platform packages (`michi-darwin-arm64`, `michi-linux-x64-musl`, etc.); that wiring isn't there yet
- ❌ **`packages/michi-node/pnpm-lock.yaml` is gitignored — never committed.** CI runs `pnpm install` with no lockfile in the checkout and no `--frozen-lockfile`, so dependency resolution is different (and unreviewed) on every run
- ❌ No release/publish CI job at all — the existing workflow only builds/tests/lints
- ⚠️ CI's napi matrix builds `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, but the design doc's actual publish target is `linux-x64-musl` — those don't match

## How you'd actually publish (once the gaps above are closed)

- **crates.io**: `cargo login <token>`, then `cargo publish -p michi`. One command, but irreversible — a published version can never be replaced or deleted, only "yanked."
- **npm**: multi-step because of the native binary — build the `.node` per target platform, run `napi prepublish -t npm` to generate the platform-specific sub-packages, `npm publish` each of those plus the root package (which carries them as `optionalDependencies`). Doing this by hand is tedious and error-prone; it's normally driven entirely by CI on a git tag, which is why the missing release workflow matters.

I won't run either of those without you explicitly asking — both are effectively one-way doors.

## Keeping it safe from hackers

In rough priority order:

1. **Commit `pnpm-lock.yaml` and add `--frozen-lockfile` to CI's `pnpm install`.** Right now npm dependency resolution isn't pinned or reviewable — this is the same class of gap as the classic "no lockfile" supply-chain issue.
2. **`crate-ci/typos@master` in `ci.yml` is pinned to a floating branch, not a version or SHA** — it's the one non-pinned action in your CI. If that branch is ever compromised, it's arbitrary code execution with access to your CI secrets. Pin it to a release tag or commit SHA.
3. More generally, pin all GitHub Actions to commit SHAs, not tags (tags can be moved) — this is the OSSF Scorecard/GitHub-recommended baseline for CI supply-chain hygiene.
4. `cargo-deny` (advisories + license bans) is already wired into CI and passing — that's good, keep it, and consider a scheduled (not just per-PR) run so newly-disclosed advisories on unchanged dependencies still get caught.
5. When you do set up publishing, prefer **Trusted Publishing** (OIDC) for both crates.io and npm over long-lived tokens stored as CI secrets — no static credential for an attacker to exfiltrate.
6. The NAPI boundary itself (untrusted JS input) got hardened in this session's review — bounds validation + `catch_unwind` on every export. That was the main "attacker-adjacent" surface in the actual code, and it's covered.

Want me to go ahead and fix the concrete, low-risk items now — add `README.md` + `LICENSE`, commit the lockfile with `--frozen-lockfile` in CI, and pin the `typos` action? The bigger items (napi cross-platform config, an actual release workflow, choosing token vs. OIDC publishing) involve some decisions I'd want your input on first.
Can we close the gaps? Any docs, readmes should be written with a friendly tone, engineering focused, scannable and devoid of AI slop and AI word salad.

# michi (道)

AXI response primitives for agent-ergonomic tools — TOON lists, key-value blocks,
truncation, structured errors, status, and `help[]` hints, in one small, pure-computation
crate.

`michi` is the primitive layer of the **orin-axi** suite. It doesn't know about your
protocol, your CLI framework, or your async runtime — it takes structured data in and
returns token-efficient, agent-readable strings out. Four tools in the suite (Monokl,
Firkin, Lumen, Pulse) build on it instead of re-implementing this formatting themselves.

Available from Rust directly, or from TypeScript via the `michi` npm package.

## Why

Agents pay for every token they read. A JSON list of even modest size burns tokens on
repeated field names and punctuation that a human reader would never notice and an LLM
doesn't need restated per row. TOON (Token-Optimized Object Notation) states field names
once, in the header:

```json
[
  { "number": 51815, "title": "[Bug]: Telegram plugin", "state": "open" },
  { "number": 51812, "title": "dark mode request", "state": "open" }
]
```

```text
issues[2]{number,title,state}:
  51815,"[Bug]: Telegram plugin",open
  51812,dark mode request,open
```

Same information, about 40% fewer tokens. That adds up fast across a long agent session.

## Quick start

```rust
use michi::toon;

#[derive(serde::Serialize)]
struct Issue {
    number: u64,
    title: String,
    state: String,
}

let issues = vec![
    Issue { number: 51815, title: "[Bug]: Telegram plugin".into(), state: "open".into() },
    Issue { number: 51812, title: "dark mode request".into(), state: "open".into() },
];

let response = toon::list("issues", &issues)
    .total(8771)
    .hint("gh-axi issue view <number>", "view an issue")
    .render();

print!("{response}");
```

```typescript
import { toon } from "michi";

const issues = [
  { number: 51815, title: "[Bug]: Telegram plugin", state: "open" },
  { number: 51812, title: "dark mode request", state: "open" },
];

const response = toon
  .list("issues", issues)
  .total(8771)
  .hint("gh-axi issue view <number>", "view an issue")
  .render();

process.stdout.write(response);
```

Both produce:

```text
count: 2 of 8771 total
issues[2]{number,title,state}:
  51815,"[Bug]: Telegram plugin",open
  51812,dark mode request,open
help[1]:
  Run `gh-axi issue view <number>` to view an issue
```

## Install

```toml
[dependencies]
michi = "0.1"
```

```bash
pnpm add michi     # or npm install / yarn add
```

Default features add zero runtime dependencies — no tokio, no async runtime, nothing
beyond `thiserror`. You opt into more as you need it (see below).

## What's in the box

| Module | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `toon` | TOON list rendering — the token-optimized agent list format |
| `kv` | Key-value single-item rendering |
| `hints` | `help[]` contextual next-step blocks |
| `truncate` | Token-safe content truncation, always on char boundaries |
| `empty` | Definitive empty-state responses (`count: 0`, never silent) |
| `error` | Unified `michi::Error` with agent-renderable output + retry classification |
| `idempotency` | Idempotency keys and already-done detection |
| `resilience` | Retry config, backoff delay calculation, `Retry-After` parsing |
| `status` | Health/status response rendering |
| `recovery` | Structured recovery hints for error responses |
| `response` | `AgentResponse` builder — composes all of the above |
| `pipeline` | Pipeline data model + rendering (execution lands in a later release) |

## Feature flags

| Feature | Adds | Why you'd enable it |
|---|---|---|
| `pipeline` | tokio, async execution types | running actual pipelines, not just rendering their state |
| `fuzzy` | nucleo-matcher | fuzzy-resolving ambiguous agent input |
| `cache` | moka, sha2 | two-tier caching with tag invalidation |
| `cli` | indicatif, inquire, crossterm, ctrlc | building a CLI surface on top of michi |
| `mcp` | (pure logic, no extra deps) | building an MCP server surface |
| `full` | everything above except `napi` | test/bench harnesses |

The default build (no features) is the one most consumers want: pure rendering, no
runtime, no surprises in your dependency tree.

## Docs

- [`docs/00-overview.md`](docs/00-overview.md) — what this is and where it fits in the suite
- [`docs/01-spec.md`](docs/01-spec.md) — full API reference and the TOON grammar
- [`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-03-michi-design.md`](docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-03-michi-design.md) — architecture decisions

## Development

```bash
just test    # rust + node tests
just check   # fmt + clippy + deny + typos
just bench   # divan benchmarks
```

See [`CLAUDE.md`](CLAUDE.md) for the full contributor ground rules.

## License

AGPL-3.0-or-later. See [`LICENSE`](LICENSE).

# michi

TypeScript/JavaScript bindings for [`michi`](https://github.com/orin-axi/michi) — AXI
response primitives for agent-ergonomic tools. Native binary via NAPI-RS, no WASM, no
JS reimplementation of the rendering logic.

## Install

```bash
pnpm add michi
```

## Quick start

```typescript
import { renderToon } from "michi";

const out = renderToon({
  typeName: "issues",
  fields: ["number", "title", "state"],
  rows: [
    [{ type: "int", intVal: 51815 }, { type: "str", strVal: "[Bug]: Telegram plugin" }, { type: "str", strVal: "open" }],
    [{ type: "int", intVal: 51812 }, { type: "str", strVal: "dark mode request" }, { type: "str", strVal: "open" }],

  totalCount: 8771,
  hints: ["Run `gh-axi issue view <number>` to view an issue"],
});

process.stdout.write(out);

issues[2]{number,title,state}:
  51815,[Bug]: Telegram plugin,open
  51812,dark mode request,open
totalCount: 8771
help[1]:
  Run `gh-axi issue view <number>` to view an issue
```

## API

| Function | Signature |
|---|---|
| `renderToon` | `(opts: JsToonOptions) => string` — TOON list rendering |
| `emptyState` | `(typeName: string) => string` — definitive empty-state block |
| `renderHints` | `(hints: string[]) => string` — `help[N]:` block |
| `truncate` | `(content: string, maxChars: number, hint: string) => string` |

Full type definitions ship in `index.d.ts`. See the
[main repo](https://github.com/orin-axi/michi) for the complete primitive set, the TOON
grammar, and the Rust API this wraps.

## Supported platforms

Prebuilt native binaries: `darwin-arm64`, `linux-x64-musl`. Building from source requires
a Rust toolchain (see [`rust-toolchain.toml`](../../rust-toolchain.toml) in the main repo).

## License

AGPL-3.0-or-later. See [`LICENSE`](LICENSE).

# Contributing to michi

Thanks for taking a look. This is a small, deliberately narrow crate — most contributions
will be a bug fix, a new primitive, or filling in a Plan 2 stub. Here's how to get moving.

## Setup

```bash
git clone git@github.com:orin-axi/michi.git
cd michi
just build
just test
```

You'll need a stable Rust toolchain (see `rust-toolchain.toml`) and, for the npm package,
`pnpm` 9+. `just` is the task runner — run `just --list` for everything available.

## Before you open a PR

```bash
just check   # fmt-check + clippy (pedantic, all features) + cargo-deny + typos
just test    # cargo nextest (rust) + node test suite
```

Both need to pass. CI runs the same checks, so this just saves you a round trip.

## Ground rules

The short version — full detail in [`CLAUDE.md`](CLAUDE.md):

- No `unwrap()`/`expect()`/`panic!` in library code (tests may use `.expect("message")`)
- No `unsafe` outside the NAPI boundary (`src/napi.rs`)
- Every `pub` item gets a doc comment
- Strings that get built up are pre-allocated with `String::with_capacity`
- Truncation always respects char boundaries — never byte-slice blindly
- Tests run via `cargo nextest`, not `cargo test`; benchmarks are `divan`, not `criterion`

These aren't arbitrary — they're what keeps a crate meant to sit under four other tools
predictable to depend on. If a rule is actively fighting you on something, say so in the
PR rather than working around it quietly; the lint config has already been tuned once
based on exactly that kind of feedback.

## Workflow

We use test-driven development for fixes and new primitives: write a test that fails for
the right reason first, then make it pass. For anything touching more than one file, a
quick look at [`ARCHITECTURE.md`](ARCHITECTURE.md) will save you some guessing about which
side of the always-compiled / feature-gated line something belongs on.

## Where things live

| You want to... | Look at |
|---|---|
| Add or change a rendering primitive | `src/<module>/` — see the module table in `README.md` |
| Touch anything behind a feature flag | `ARCHITECTURE.md` for the feature graph first |
| Change the NAPI/npm surface | `src/napi.rs` (the exports) + `packages/michi-node` (the cdylib shim) — not the other way around |
| Update the TOON grammar or wire format | `docs/01-spec.md` is the source of truth; keep it and `src/toon/` in sync |
| Understand *why* something is shaped the way it is | `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-03-michi-design.md` |

## Commit messages

Short, imperative, prefixed by kind — `fix:`, `feat:`, `chore:`, `test:`, `style:`,
`ci:`. Look at `git log --oneline` for the house style before your first commit.

## Reporting bugs

Open a GitHub issue. If it's security-sensitive (something exploitable at the NAPI
boundary, a dependency advisory, etc.), say so in the title and we'll prioritize
accordingly — this is a young project without a formal disclosure process yet.

# Architecture This is the "how it fits together today" doc. For the reasoning behind these choices, see [`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-03-michi-design.md`](docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-03-michi-design.md). For the full module list and public API, see `README.md` and [`docs/01-spec.md`](docs/01-spec.md). This doc only covers structure. ## One crate, feature-gated `michi` ships as a single crate with everything behind opt-in features rather than as several small crates. A consumer who adds `michi` with default features gets pure rendering and nothing else — no async runtime, no cache, no CLI deps. That guarantee is enforced by Cargo, not by convention: each feature only exists to unlock `optional = true` dependencies that nothing in the default build ever references. ```mermaid flowchart LR fuzzy --> pipeline cache --> pipeline cli --> pipeline mcp --> pipeline pipeline --> tokio[("tokio + tokio-util
+ async-trait + uuid")] napi --> napideps[("napi + napi-derive")] ``` The one thing worth internalizing from this graph: **`fuzzy`, `cache`, `cli`, and `mcp` all pull in `pipeline`, and `pipeline` is what pulls in tokio.** Want fuzzy matching with no async runtime? Not possible today — `Resolution` is used in pipeline context, so `fuzzy` implies `pipeline` by design. `napi` is the only feature that's a dead end on its own — it never touches tokio. ## Two crates, one build-artifact boundary `packages/michi-node` exists as a second Cargo crate for exactly one reason: `crate-type = ["cdylib"]` can't coexist with a regular `[lib]` in the same `Cargo.toml`. It is not a second layer of design — it's a thin shim. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph michi["michi (rlib)"] core["always-compiled modules
toon, kv, hints, error, ..."] napi_mod["src/napi.rs
#[cfg(feature = \"napi\")]"] end subgraph node["packages/michi-node (cdylib)"] shim["src/lib.rs:
pub use michi::napi::*;"] end napi_mod --> shim shim --> binary[(".node binary")] binary --> npm["npm package \"michi\"
(TypeScript consumers)"] ``` Every `#[napi]` export — the actual function bodies, the `JsToonOptions` / `JsToonValue` types, the input-bounds validation — lives in `src/napi.rs`, inside the main crate, where it's unit-tested like everything else. `packages/michi-node/src/lib.rs` does nothing but `pub use michi::napi::*;`. **If you're adding a NAPI export, it goes in `src/napi.rs`, not in `packages/michi-node`.** The re-export still works because napi-derive's registration is linker-section based (`ctor`), not call-site based — it survives crossing a crate boundary via `pub use`. This is verified by an actual `.node` build + the JS test suite in CI, not just `cargo build`. ## Always-compiled vs. feature-gated, inside one module The pattern used throughout: pure, sync computation is always compiled; the async extension of the same concept sits behind a feature, in the same directory. ``` resilience/ mod.rs next_retry_delay(), parse_retry_after() ← always compiled policy.rs with_resilience() ← #[cfg(feature = "pipeline")] circuit.rs CircuitBreaker, CircuitState ← #[cfg(feature = "pipeline")] pipeline/ mod.rs Pipeline (pure data) + render() ← always compiled executor.rs PipelineExecutor, PipelineContext ← #[cfg(feature = "pipeline")] ``` `pipeline::Pipeline` is deliberately always compiled: a caller should be able to render a pipeline's current state without pulling in an executor to run one. The same split applies to `resilience` (you can compute a retry delay without tokio) and will apply to `sink` once Plan 2 fills it in. ## Boundaries worth knowing before you touch them - **`src/napi.rs` is the one place `unsafe` is permitted** (`#![deny(unsafe_code)]` at the crate root, with a scoped `#![allow(unsafe_code)]` inside `napi.rs` for napi-derive's generated FFI glue — `deny`, not `forbid`, specifically so that override is possible). - **Untrusted input crosses exactly one boundary**: JS callers, via NAPI. Every export there validates collection sizes before doing work and is wrapped in `#[napi(catch_unwind)]`. Nowhere else in the crate needs to think about adversarial input — callers elsewhere are trusted Rust code. - **`docs/01-spec.md`'s TOON grammar is the contract.** If you change what `escape_value` or `render_toon` produce, update the spec in the same PR — they're supposed to describe the same thing.

All the gaps are closed and verified. Quick correction on one thing from my earlier audit, plus a summary:

**Correction:** `pnpm-lock.yaml` was actually already committed to git (`.gitignore` doesn't retroactively untrack a file) — so the risk wasn't "no lockfile in CI," it was that plain `pnpm install` would silently rewrite the lockfile on drift instead of failing loudly. Fixed by adding `--frozen-lockfile`, and I removed the now-dead `.gitignore` line.

**What's done, all verified (`just check`, `cargo publish --dry-run`, actual builds):**
- `README.md` (root) + `packages/michi-node/README.md` — quick starts are the *real*, verified-working API (I caught that the overview doc's example was explicitly aspirational/illustrative, not what `render_toon`/`ToonOptions` actually look like today — ran both the Rust and Node examples for real before writing them down)
- `LICENSE` (full AGPL-3.0 text, fetched from gnu.org) in both the root and `packages/michi-node`
- `Cargo.toml` now has `readme = "README.md"` so crates.io actually renders it
- CI: pinned `crate-ci/typos@master` → a commit SHA (`v1.48.0`), added `--frozen-lockfile` to both `pnpm install` steps
- `CONTRIBUTING.md` — setup, ground rules (linking to `CLAUDE.md` rather than duplicating it), where things live, commit style
- `ARCHITECTURE.md` — two Mermaid diagrams, both earning their place: the feature-flag graph (makes the "fuzzy/cache/cli/mcp all silently pull in tokio via `pipeline`; `napi` doesn't" relationship obvious at a glance) and the two-crate/NAPI re-export flow (the exact thing someone would get wrong if they added a new NAPI export in the wrong crate)

Nothing's committed yet — want me to commit this batch?
What do we have a TS package for? Should this just be a crate or do we want to provide more of a interface for TS/JS CLIs and MCPs?

Today it's not "the crate, in TS" — it's a thin slice. The npm package wraps exactly 4 functions (`renderToon`, `emptyState`, `renderHints`, `truncate`). `kv`, `error`, `status`, `recovery`, `resilience`, `idempotency`, and — notably — the `AgentResponse` builder (the actual top-level thing that composes body + hints + recovery + output format) have **zero** TS bindings. That's already a gap against what `docs/00-overview.md`'s own suite table promises: Firkin wants "structured error output," Lumen wants "status + hint primitives," and neither is reachable from TypeScript right now.

My lean: expand it, but selectively — wrap the primitives that have real logic worth sharing (`error` classification, `status`, `recovery`, and especially `AgentResponse` as the actual entry point), and skip the ones trivial enough that a TS reimplementation costs nothing (`idempotency` is just an `Option` check). The concrete argument for *sharing* rather than letting TS reimplement: this review just fixed a real jitter/cap bug in `resilience` and a real escaping bug in `toon` — logic subtle enough to get wrong once. A TS reimplementation doesn't inherit that hardening; it's a second place the same class of bug can reappear independently.

The thing that actually decides this, though, isn't something I can see from the code:

questions.question: Are Firkin/Lumen (the suite tools that specifically need error/status output) themselves written in TypeScript, or are they Rust tools that'll consume the crate directly?

options.label: TS/JS (MCP servers, CLIs)

content.text:
Good — that changes the calculus. Since Firkin/Lumen consume the crate directly as Rust, there's no internal pressure forcing TS parity. That reframes the npm package's job: it's not "the crate, minus what we haven't ported yet," it's a deliberately scoped surface for *external* TS/JS consumers (third-party MCP servers, TS CLIs) who don't want to reimplement TOON's escaping/grammar in JS themselves.

Given that, I'd walk back my earlier lean — **the current 4-function scope (`renderToon`, `emptyState`, `renderHints`, `truncate`) is close to the right MVP, not a gap.** Those are exactly the primitives worth sharing:

- `toon`/`truncate` have real logic (escaping, char-boundary safety) that's genuinely worth not reimplementing per-language
- `kv`, `hints`, `empty` are trivial enough that a TS consumer loses nothing writing them by hand if they ever need them
- `error`/`status`/`recovery`/`response` (the builder) encode *michi's own opinions* about error classification and response shape — a TS-based MCP server likely has its own error model already, and forcing michi's onto it is exactly the kind of speculative-generality this review kept flagging elsewhere (recall the `IdempotencyKey` finding)

So: **build out more NAPI surface only when an actual external TS consumer asks for something specific**, not preemptively. YAGNI applies here now that "the suite needs it" isn't the driver.

One concrete thing worth fixing given this: the README's opening line — *"Available from Rust directly, or from TypeScript via the `michi` npm package"* — reads like it's promising parity it doesn't have. Want me to soften that to be honest about scope (something like "core list-rendering primitives also available from TypeScript"), or would you rather leave the framing as-is and just let the npm README's own function table speak for itself?

Good — "MCP v2" isn't ambiguous, it's the actual TypeScript SDK's v2 (implementing the 2026-07-28 spec revision, currently in beta). I pulled the actual server guide docs rather than going from memory, and it changes the answer in a useful way.

**The one thing actually worth exposing: `AgentResponse` maps almost exactly onto MCP's `CallToolResult`.**

A v2 tool result is `{ content: [{type: 'text', text}], isError?: boolean, structuredContent?: object }`. Tool errors aren't a separate channel — they're just `isError: true` on an ordinary result, with the recovery hint living in `text` because "it's the only thing the model has to work with" (their words, and it's exactly what `help[]` blocks already are). `AgentResponse.render(Text)` already concatenates body + hints + recovery into one string, and `.is_error` is already a bool. So a TS MCP tool handler built on michi collapses to:

```ts
return { content: [{ type: 'text', text: resp.render() }], isError: resp.isError };
```

That's a much more targeted case for NAPI exposure than the general "wrap everything" argument from before — this isn't speculative, it's a near-exact shape match. `kv` is worth adding alongside it for the same reason `toon` already is.

**What shouldn't come from michi:** MCP's own error vocabulary — `ProtocolError`/`ProtocolErrorCode`, the `-32xxx` wire codes. Those only apply to resource/prompt/completion callbacks (tools only ever produce `isError: true`, never a protocol error), and they're exactly the "protocol knowledge" the crate already deliberately excludes. `michi::ErrorClass` (User/Internal/Transient) is a different, complementary axis — useful for a caller deciding *whether* to retry, not for picking a wire code — and shouldn't try to grow into one.

**One forward-looking connection worth knowing about, not acting on yet:** v2 moves long-running tool calls to Tasks — the server returns a task handle, the client polls `tasks/get`/`tasks/update`. `pipeline::Pipeline` (step list + `Completed`/`Skipped`/`Failed`/`Pending` status) is already shaped to render exactly that kind of progress state. That's a second concrete NAPI case, but it's gated on Plan 2's executor actually existing — not relevant today.

`structuredContent` (the schema-validated parallel JSON) doesn't need anything new either — a TS caller has the raw array before it calls `renderToon`, so it can hand that same data to `structuredContent` independently.

Want to actually scope this out (add `AgentResponse` + `kv` to the NAPI surface), or is this still just mapping the territory for now?

1	# michi — Specification
2	> orin-axi · Draft · June 2026
3	
4	---
5	
6	## Overview
7	
8	`michi` is a Rust crate of pure agentic response primitives — the
9	conventions that make tools ergonomic for LLMs regardless of protocol or
10	language. It is general-purpose: useful to anyone building AXI-compliant
11	tools, not tied to any specific stack.
12	
13	AXI (Agent eXperience Interface) is a set of ten design principles for
14	agent-ergonomic tooling that treats token budget as a first-class constraint.
15	Its thesis is that the "MCP vs. CLI" debate is the wrong frame: the real
16	question is which design principles make *any* interface effective for an LLM
17	agent. A well-designed interface following these principles measurably
18	outperforms both naive CLIs and MCP on task success rate, cost, duration, and
19	number of turns. `michi` encodes the subset of those principles that are pure,
20	language-agnostic computation — the parts that benefit from a single canonical,
21	tested implementation rather than ad-hoc re-derivation in every tool.
22	
23	It encodes **seven of the ten AXI principles** as typed, tested Rust: TOON
24	list rendering, key-value single-item rendering, contextual disclosure
25	(`help[]`), pre-computed aggregates (`totalCount`), content truncation,
26	definitive empty states, structured errors with exit codes, idempotency
27	signals, retry delay primitives, and content-first status responses.
28	
29	| AXI principle | michi module(s) |
30	|---|---|
31	| **P1 — Token-Efficient Output** | `toon`, `kv` |
32	| **P3 — Content Truncation** | `truncate` |
33	| **P4 — Pre-Computed Aggregates** | `ToonOptions::total_count` (the `totalCount:` line), `status` health summaries |
34	| **P5 — Definitive Empty States** | `empty` |
35	| **P6 — Structured Errors & Exit Codes** | `error`, `idempotency` |
36	| **P8 — Content First** | `status` |
37	| **P9 — Contextual Disclosure** | `hints`, `recovery` |
38	
39	The three remaining principles are deliberately out of scope: **P2 — Minimal
40	Default Schemas** is supported (callers pass exactly the fields they want) but
41	not enforced; **P7 — Ambient Context** and **P10 — Consistent Help** are
42	session-hook and CLI-framework concerns that live in the consuming tool, not in
43	a pure rendering crate.
44	
45	The crate has no protocol knowledge (no MCP, no HTTP, no CLI framework) and
46	no async runtime dependency. It is pure computation: data in, strings and types
47	out. TypeScript consumers reach it via the NAPI npm wrapper `michi`. Rust
48	consumers take a direct crates.io or git dep.
49	
50	---
51	
52	## Motivation
53	
54	AXI's ten design principles describe how to build agent-ergonomic interfaces,
55	but the principles themselves are typically implemented ad-hoc — scattered as
56	TypeScript conventions in MCP servers, implicit CLI output patterns, and
57	per-tool string formatting that drifts over time. When `michi` exists:
58	
59	- The TOON format has a canonical, tested Rust implementation shared by both
60	  MCP and CLI consumers
61	- `help[]` hint construction, `totalCount` formatting, truncation signals, and
62	  recovery hint shapes are defined once and cannot drift between consumers
63	- Any agent-facing Rust CLI can import the same primitives directly
64	- Any TypeScript MCP server or CLI can reach them via the NAPI npm package
65	
66	A non-agentic tool (infrastructure CLIs, build scripts) uses its own output
67	conventions and never encounters michi. The package boundary enforces the
68	separation — agentic concepts do not leak into infrastructure.
69	
70	---
71	
72	## Non-goals
73	
74	- **Display-format Markdown** — research-grounded LLM display formatters
75	  (fields, sections, tables) are the caller's concern. michi is the
76	  `audience: ["assistant"]` compact surface; display rendering for the
77	  `audience: ["user"]` surface stays in your MCP SDK or application layer.
78	- **MCP protocol knowledge** — no `content[]`, no `outputSchema`, no
79	  `structuredContent`. Those are assembled by the calling MCP framework.
80	- **CLI framework** — no argument parsing, no stdin/stdout handling. That
81	  belongs to the caller's CLI framework of choice.
82	- **HTTP client** — no auth handling, no request construction. michi
83	  provides retry delay primitives that a caller plugs into their own HTTP
84	  client.
85	- **Async runtime** — zero tokio, zero async-std. All functions are sync
86	  and pure. Callers own retry loops and timeout semantics.
87	- **Full retry implementation** — michi provides `RetryConfig`,
88	  `parse_retry_after()`, and `next_retry_delay()`. The actual retry loop
89	  (sleep + re-execute) stays in the caller.
90	- **Caching** — callers should use `moka` or equivalent. michi does not
91	  include a cache.
92	- **Logging / telemetry** — Rust consumers use the `tracing` crate
93	  independently.
94	- **Schema validation** — input validation is the caller's concern.
95	- **MCP server bootstrapping** — `server.tool()`, tool discovery, deferred
96	  loading. Protocol-specific, stays in your MCP SDK.
97	
98	---
99	
100	## Consumer map
101	
102	```
103	Any Rust CLI binary
104	  Cargo.toml dep on michi (crates.io or git)
105	  Render --format toon via michi::render_toon()
106	  Full access to all modules — no NAPI overhead
107	
108	Any TypeScript CLI
109	  npm dep on michi
110	  --format toon dispatch calls into NAPI wrapper
111	  Same output; NAPI boundary is transparent
112	
113	Any TypeScript MCP server
114	  npm dep on michi
115	  Renders TOON for audience:["assistant"] content block
116	  Assembles MCP content[] from the returned string
117	```
118	
119	---
120	
121	## Cargo.toml
122	
123	```toml
124	[package]
125	name = "michi"
126	version = "0.1.0"
127	edition = "2021"
128	rust-version = "1.93"
129	description = "AXI response primitives for agent-ergonomic tools"
130	license = "AGPL-3.0-or-later"
131	repository = "https://github.com/orin-axi/michi"
132	keywords = ["axi", "agent", "mcp", "cli", "llm"]
133	categories = ["text-processing", "encoding", "development-tools"]
134	
135	[features]

1190	| Retry-After header parsing | Ad-hoc string parsing | `resilience::parse_retry_after()` |
1191	| Retryable status classification | Hardcoded booleans per caller | `resilience::is_retryable_status()` |
1192	| Error classification shape | Ad-hoc per tool | `error::AxiError`, `error::ErrorCode` |
1193	| Empty state handling | Ad-hoc per tool (often silent) | `empty::empty_state()` |
1194	| Truncation | Ad-hoc per tool, no standard signal | `truncate::truncate()`, `truncate_inline()` |
1195	
1196	### Genuinely new — does not exist as a shared primitive today
1197	
1198	| What | Why |
1199	|---|---|
1200	| TOON renderer | New format — token-efficient list encoding for agent context windows |
1201	| `kv::render_kv()` | Single-item Markdown-KV with aligned columns; no standard Rust equivalent |
1202	| `status::StatusResponse` | Typed P8 content-first orientation response — novel primitive |
1203	| `idempotency::already_done()` | Typed already-done signal with canonical output format |
1204	| `idempotency::PartialSuccess` | General partial-success reporting with per-op recovery hints |
1205	| `idempotency::IdempotencyKey` | Canonical key construction with stable hashing |
1206	| `AgentResponse` builder | Unified construction API across all consumers |

1403	### `AgentResponse` format routing
1404	
1405	The builder routes to TOON or KV based on which items method the caller uses,
1406	not on item count. The caller is responsible for choosing the right format:
1407	
1408	```rust
1409	// List of uniform-schema items → TOON

1470	429 and 50x gateway errors (502, 503, 504) represent transient conditions —
1471	rate limits and upstream unavailability — where the same request is likely to
1472	succeed after a delay. 500 represents a server-side bug. Retrying a 500 without
1473	changing anything about the request will produce the same 500. Worse, retrying
1474	write operations that returned 500 may produce duplicate side effects if the
1475	server processed the request before erroring.
1476	
1477	Callers that genuinely need to retry 500s (some APIs use it for transient
1478	conditions) can implement their own `is_retryable` predicate and pass it to
1479	their retry loop independently of `is_retryable_status()`.
1480	
1481	```rust
1482	// Default: 429, 502, 503, 504 only
1483	if is_retryable_status(status) { ... }
1484	
1485	// Custom: caller adds 500 for a specific API known to use it transiently
1486	let retryable = is_retryable_status(status) || status == 500;
1487	```

1490	
1491	### `render_hints_only()` — the three-surface seam
1492	
1493	This method exists to support MCP frameworks that implement a three-surface
1494	response pattern: one content block for agent consumption
1495	(`audience: ["assistant"]`), one for display (`audience: ["user"]`), and a
1496	`structuredContent` payload for client tooling. In this pattern, the display
1497	body is rendered via the framework's own Markdown or rich-text layer, while the
1498	agent-facing block combines TOON output with a `help[]` trailer.
1499	
1500	Without `render_hints_only()`, framework code that has already rendered a
1501	display body would need to reconstruct an `AgentResponse` just to get a
1502	formatted `help[]` block to append to the agent surface.
1503	
1504	```typescript
1505	// Example: MCP framework TypeScript (simplified)
1506	function assembleToolResult(opts: RespondOpts): ToolResult {
1507	  const userBody      = renderDisplayMarkdown(opts.body);    // display surface → audience:["user"]
1508	  const hintsBlock    = michi.renderHintsOnly(opts.hints);   // michi → append to assistant body
1509	  const assistantBody = opts.assistant                       // caller-provided TOON
1510	      ?? (userBody + "\n" + hintsBlock);                     // fallback: display body + hints
1511	
1512	  return {
1513	    content: [
1514	      { type: "text", text: assistantBody,
1515	        annotations: { audience: ["assistant"], priority: 1.0 } },
1516	      { type: "text", text: userBody,
1517	        annotations: { audience: ["user"],      priority: 0.5 } },
1518	    ],
1519	    structuredContent: opts.structured ?? null,
1520	  };
1521	}
1522	```
1523	
1524	`render_hints_only()` is the narrow seam between michi and the calling
1525	framework's rendering layer — it allows the `help[]` format to be owned by
1526	Rust without requiring the framework to understand TOON.

1576	### `outputSchema` is in the LLM context
1577	
1578	A precision point that matters for token budget planning in MCP servers that

1581	- **`outputSchema`** on a tool definition is part of the `tools/list` response.

225	## TOON format specification
226	
227	TOON (Token-Optimized Object Notation) is the agent-facing list format.
228	It front-loads structure (type, count, field names) so the LLM has full
229	context before reading any row, then encodes rows as compact comma-separated
230	values. Field names appear once in the header rather than once per row.
231	
232	This is the canonical implementation of **AXI Principle 1 (Token-Efficient
233	Output)**: every token in a response permanently consumes context-window
234	budget, and on multi-turn tasks that cost compounds across turns. TOON omits
235	the braces, quotes, and repeated keys that JSON spends on structure the LLM can
236	already infer positionally.
237	
238	**Why TOON for lists?**
239	Standard JSON repeats field names on every item. Markdown key-value format
240	repeats field names per item, which is ideal for single items and small sets
241	but expensive at scale. TOON trades per-item field repetition for a one-time
242	header, saving proportionally more tokens as N grows. For lists of 5+ items,
243	TOON is the better token budget choice. For single items or small metadata
244	blocks, key-value format remains preferred — see `kv::render_kv()`.
245	
246	AXI's benchmark shows this class of output optimization delivers approximately
247	40% token reduction over equivalent JSON for list data.
248	
249	### Grammar
250	
251	```
252	document     ::= type_header NEWLINE row+ totalcount? help_block?
253	type_header  ::= type_name "[" count "]" "{" field_list "}" ":"
254	type_name    ::= [a-z_][a-z0-9_]*                 (snake_case)
255	count        ::= [0-9]+                            (items in this response)
256	field_list   ::= field_name ("," field_name)*
257	field_name   ::= [a-z_][a-z0-9_]*
258	row          ::= "  " value ("," value)* NEWLINE   (2-space indent)
259	value        ::= scalar | quoted
260	scalar       ::= [^,\n"]*
261	quoted       ::= '"' ( [^"\\] | "\\" . )* '"'     (for values with commas)
262	totalcount   ::= "totalCount: " [0-9]+ NEWLINE     (total available, may exceed count)
263	help_block   ::= "help[" [0-9]+ "]:" NEWLINE hint+
264	hint         ::= "  " [^\n]+ NEWLINE
265	```
266	
267	### Examples
268	
269	**List response:**
270	```
271	issues[3]{number,title,state}:
272	  42,Fix login redirect,open
273	  43,Add dark mode,open
274	  44,"Update deps, bump major",closed
275	totalCount: 47
276	help[2]:
277	  Call get_issue with number=<number> for full detail
278	  Call list_issues with state=open to filter
279	```
280	
281	**Truncated field value:**
282	```
283	components[2]{name,description,tokens}:
284	  Button,"Primary action element (148 chars truncated — use full=true)",12
285	  Icon,"Scalable vector icon (203 chars truncated — use full=true)",8
286	totalCount: 84
287	help[1]:
288	  Call get_component with name=<name> and full=true for complete description
289	```
290	
291	**Empty state:**
292	```
293	issues[0]{}:
294	totalCount: 0
295	help[1]:
296	  Try list_issues with a broader filter
297	```
298	
299	**Single recovery hint (no list):**
300	```
301	help[1]:
302	  Retry create_item with suggestedParams: { project: "PROJ", type: "Task" }
303	```
304	
305	### Escaping rules
306	
307	- Values containing commas MUST be quoted
308	- Values containing double-quote characters use backslash escape: `\"`
309	- Values containing newlines MUST be truncated before rendering — TOON
310	  does not support multi-line cell values
311	- Null/absent values render as empty scalar: `val1,,val3`
312	- Boolean values: `true` / `false` literals
313	- Numeric values: rendered without quotes

461	Implements **AXI Principle 9 (Contextual Disclosure)**: after every output,

464	the current context, but leave runtime values as named placeholders (`<id>`)

498	single verbose field can otherwise consume thousands of tokens, exhausting the
499	context budget before the agent has read the rest of a list; truncation
500	preserves enough signal for most operations while reserving budget for
501	subsequent turns.

509	    pub signal:       Option<String>,

546	### `error` — structured errors with exit codes
547	
548	Implements **AXI Principle 6 (Structured Errors and Exit Codes)**: errors are
549	written to **stdout** (not stderr), carry a clean exit code (`0` success, `1`
550	error), carry recovery hints, and never block on interactive prompts. Agents
551	cannot answer `Are you sure? [y/n]`, may not capture stderr at all, and cannot
552	reliably parse freeform error text. `AxiError` encodes the structured contract
553	as a type.
554	
555	The HTTP status → `ErrorCode` mapping is NOT in michi — callers produce an
556	`ErrorCode` after interpreting whatever failure occurred. This keeps the
557	module free of HTTP knowledge.
558	
559	```rust
560	#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
561	pub struct AxiError {
562	    pub code:        ErrorCode,
563	    pub message:     String,
564	    pub hints:       Vec<Hint>,
565	    pub recovery:    Option<RecoveryHint>,
566	    pub retryable:   bool,
567	    pub retry_after: Option<std::time::Duration>,
568	}
569	
570	impl std::fmt::Display for AxiError {
571	    // delegates to render()
572	}
573	
574	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
575	pub enum ErrorCode {
576	    // Non-retryable — agent should not retry without changing params
577	    InvalidInput,    // bad parameters
578	    NotFound,        // resource absent
579	    Unauthorized,    // auth failure
580	    Forbidden,       // permission denied
581	    Conflict,        // resource state mismatch
582	
583	    // Retryable — agent may retry same call
584	    RateLimited,     // 429 — check retry_after
585	    Unavailable,     // 503
586	    Timeout,         // request timed out
587	    ExternalFailure, // downstream error
588	}
589	
590	impl AxiError {
591	    pub fn new(code: ErrorCode, message: impl Into<String>) -> Self
592	    pub fn hint(mut self, hint: impl Into<String>) -> Self
593	    pub fn recovery(mut self, r: RecoveryHint) -> Self
594	    pub fn retry_after(mut self, d: std::time::Duration) -> Self
595	
596	    /// Render to stdout-ready string with hints attached.
597	    pub fn render(&self) -> String
598	
599	    /// AXI exit codes: 0 = success/already_done, 1 = all other errors.
600	    /// Callers should not invent additional codes.
601	    pub fn exit_code(&self) -> i32
602	}
603	```

605	The `thiserror::Error` derive plus the `Display` impl (which delegates to
606	`render()`) make `AxiError` usable with `?` in ordinary Rust call sites.

609	`ErrorCode` renders as snake_case. `render()` produces a KV-shaped block on

626	and partial-success reporting. This is the mutation-safety half of **AXI P6**:
627	write operations must be idempotent so an agent can confidently retry a
628	transient failure without duplicating records. The caller owns the persistence
629	layer that tracks what has been done; michi provides the rendering contract.

688

703	The exit code is `1` because `failed` is non-empty.

707	### `resilience` — retry delay primitives
708	
709	Pure computation only — no async, no network, no sleep. Callers build the
710	actual retry loop; michi provides the delay calculation and header parsing.
711	
712	```rust
713	pub struct RetryConfig {
714	    pub max_attempts:   u32,
715	    pub initial_delay:  std::time::Duration,
716	    pub max_delay:      std::time::Duration,
717	    pub backoff_factor: f64,
718	    pub jitter:         bool,
719	}
720	
721	impl Default for RetryConfig {
722	    fn default() -> Self {
723	        Self {
724	            max_attempts:   3,
725	            initial_delay:  std::time::Duration::from_secs(1),
726	            max_delay:      std::time::Duration::from_secs(30),
727	            backoff_factor: 2.0,
728	            jitter:         true,
729	        }
730	    }
731	}
732	
733	/// Parse a Retry-After header value.
734	/// Accepts integer seconds ("120") or HTTP-date ("Wed, 21 Oct 2026 07:28:00 GMT").
735	/// Returns None for malformed or absent values.
736	pub fn parse_retry_after(value: &str) -> Option<std::time::Duration>
737	
738	/// Compute the next retry delay.
739	/// Applies exponential backoff, optional jitter, and clamps to max_delay.
740	/// Respects retry_after when provided — returns the larger of backoff and header.
741	/// Always returns at least initial_delay.
742	pub fn next_retry_delay(
743	    attempt: u32,
744	    config: &RetryConfig,
745	    retry_after: Option<std::time::Duration>,
746	) -> std::time::Duration
747	
748	/// Whether a status code is conventionally retryable.
749	/// Returns true for: 429, 502, 503, 504.
750	/// 500 is intentionally excluded — see supplement for rationale.
751	pub fn is_retryable_status(status: u16) -> bool
752	```
753	
754	Usage pattern for a caller implementing their own retry loop:
755	```rust
756	let config = RetryConfig::default();
757	for attempt in 0..config.max_attempts {
758	    match call_api() {
759	        Ok(result) => return Ok(result),
760	        Err(e) if michi::resilience::is_retryable_status(e.status) => {
761	            let retry_after = e.retry_after_header
762	                .and_then(|h| michi::resilience::parse_retry_after(&h));
763	            let delay = michi::resilience::next_retry_delay(attempt, &config, retry_after);
764	            sleep(delay).await;
765	        }
766	        Err(e) => return Err(e),
767	    }
768	}
769	```

773	### `status` — content-first orientation responses (P8)
774	
775	Implements **AXI Principle 8 (Content First)**: a bare tool invocation shows
776	live, actionable state, not a help-text wall. When an agent invokes a tool for
777	the first time it almost always wants current state (open issues, recent PRs,
778	CI status), so serving data instead of help collapses "orient + query" into a
779	single invocation. `StatusResponse` is what any tool returns when called with
780	no arguments.

893	    pub fn total_count(mut self, n: u64) -> Self

900	    pub fn hints(mut self, hints: Vec<Hint>) -> Self

915	
916	The `items` (TOON) and `single_item` (KV) slots are stored independently, so
917	the two paths never conflict at the data level. Each render method reads only
918	its own slot: `render_toon()` uses `items`/`fields`, `render_kv()` uses
919	`single_item`. If a caller populates both and then calls `render(OutputFormat)`,
920	the requested format wins and the other slot is ignored — calling both setters
921	on one builder is a caller-side logic error, not a panic. See the supplement
922	for the recommended discipline.

925	
926	## NAPI npm package — `michi`
927	
928	The npm package is a thin napi-rs wrapper around the same crate, built with the
929	`napi` feature enabled. It follows the standard napi-rs dual-crate pattern:
930	
931	- Feature-gated `Cargo.toml` with the `napi` feature
932	- `napi-rs` with `napi-derive` proc-macros — clean Rust in, C-ABI glue and
933	  TypeScript types out, generated at compile time
934	- `serde_json::Value` for the dynamic FFI boundary (cell values, recovery params)
935	- Platform-aware binary loading via the generated `index.js`
936	- TypeScript fallback export for environments without the native binary
937	- Cross-compiled via `cargo-zigbuild`:
938	  - `aarch64-apple-darwin` (`darwin-arm64`)
939	  - `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` (`linux-x64-musl`)
940	
941	### Why the `napi4` feature
942	
943	napi-rs gates capabilities behind Node-API version features. `napi4` is the
944	lowest level that exposes `ThreadsafeFunction` and the async support napi-rs
945	needs — below it you cannot use `async fn` at the boundary at all. Node.js 12
946	(the first LTS with full napi4) is the floor; in practice every modern Node
947	target (18+) satisfies it. michi's exports are synchronous pure functions, so
948	`napi4` is comfortably sufficient and avoids pulling in niche higher-level
949	features. (napi-rs v3 is also an option and removes the old Docker-image
950	requirement for cross-compilation; the crate pins napi v2 today and can move to
951	v3 without API changes.)
952	
953	### The builder boundary problem and its solution
954	
955	This is the one genuinely hard part of wrapping michi in napi-rs, and it is
956	worth spelling out. The Rust `AgentResponse` is a **consuming** builder — every
957	setter takes `self` by value and returns `Self`:
958	
959	```rust
960	pub fn items(mut self, rows: Vec<Vec<Value>>, fields: &[&str]) -> Self
961	```
962	
963	That idiom cannot cross the napi boundary directly. A `#[napi]` class instance
964	is owned by the JavaScript garbage collector; Rust only ever receives `&self`
965	or `&mut self`, never ownership, because a live JS reference still points at the
966	underlying struct. You therefore cannot write `pub fn items(self, ...) -> Self`
967	on a napi class.
968	
969	The canonical fix is to store the consuming Rust builder in an `Option` slot and
970	`std::mem::take` it out on each mutation, applying the consuming method and
971	storing the result back:
972	
973	```rust
974	#[napi(js_name = "AgentResponse")]
975	pub struct JsAgentResponse {
976	    inner: Option<michi::AgentResponse>,
977	}
978	
979	#[napi]
980	impl JsAgentResponse {
981	    #[napi(constructor)]
982	    pub fn new(type_name: String) -> Self {
983	        Self { inner: Some(michi::AgentResponse::new(type_name)) }
984	    }

985	
986	    /// `&mut self` setter: take the consuming builder out of the Option,
987	    /// apply the consuming method, put the result back.
988	    #[napi]
989	    pub fn items(
990	        &mut self,
991	        rows: Vec<Vec<serde_json::Value>>,
992	        fields: Vec<String>,
993	    ) -> napi::Result<()> {
994	        let b = self.inner.take()
995	            .ok_or_else(|| napi::Error::from_reason("response already rendered"))?;
996	        let field_refs: Vec<&str> = fields.iter().map(String::as_str).collect();
997	        let converted = convert_rows(rows)?;            // serde_json::Value → michi::Value
998	        self.inner = Some(b.items(converted, &field_refs));
999	        Ok(())
1000	    }
1001	
1002	    #[napi]
1003	    pub fn render_toon(&self) -> napi::Result<String> {
1004	        self.inner.as_ref()
1005	            .ok_or_else(|| napi::Error::from_reason("response already consumed"))
1006	            .map(|b| b.render_toon())
1007	    }
1008	}
1009	```
1010	
1011	The `Option` acts as a nullable ownership slot: `take()` moves the value out and
1012	leaves `None`, the consuming method runs, and the result is reassigned. The
1013	TypeScript surface presents these as chainable `this`-returning setters; the
1014	wrapper realizes the chaining by mutating in place and returning the same
1015	receiver object. (Note: async `&mut self` is unsound in napi-rs — it cannot
1016	enforce exclusivity across the event loop — and would require an `unsafe`
1017	marker. michi's setters are all synchronous, so this does not arise.)
1018	
1019	### Error handling at the boundary
1020	
1021	Any `#[napi]` function returning `napi::Result<T>` throws a JS `Error` on
1022	`Err`. Two practices apply to michi:
1023	
1024	- Wrap fallible conversions (row shape mismatches, oversized inputs) in
1025	  `Result` and surface them as `napi::Error::from_reason(...)`.
1026	- Annotate exports that call into non-trivial rendering with
1027	  `#[napi(catch_unwind)]`. Without it, **a Rust panic crashes the entire Node
1028	  process** — there is no isolation boundary. With it, a panic becomes a thrown
1029	  JS `Error` (or a rejected `Promise` for async) instead of process death.
1030	
1031	### Numeric boundary gotcha
1032	
1033	`total_count` is `u64` in Rust, but JavaScript numbers are 64-bit floats with a
1034	max safe integer of 2^53. The wrapper accepts `total_count` as a JS `number`
1035	(`i64`/`number` mapping) rather than exposing raw `u64`; counts beyond 2^53 are
1036	not a realistic concern for agent list responses, and staying on `number` keeps
1037	the TypeScript ergonomic. Use explicit `BigInt` only if a consumer genuinely
1038	needs counts above the safe-integer ceiling.
1039	
1040	### Platform binary loading (`index.js`)
1041	
1042	`@napi-rs/cli` generates `index.js` at build time. It tries a locally compiled
1043	`.node` file first (so `napi build` during development needs no reinstall), then
1044	falls back to the per-platform optional-dependency npm package matching the
1045	current `process.platform` / `process.arch`. On Linux it additionally branches
1046	on glibc vs musl via `detect-libc`. Each platform binary ships as its own npm
1047	package listed under `optionalDependencies`, with `cpu`/`os` fields so package
1048	managers install only the matching one. If neither a local `.node` nor an
1049	optional dep is present, the require throws — there is no silent degradation, so
1050	the package's TypeScript fallback export should surface a clear error.
1051	
1052	> Known pitfall: npm sometimes omits optional platform deps from
1053	> `package-lock.json` when the lockfile was generated on a different
1054	> architecture (npm/cli#4828). Prefer `pnpm`, or regenerate the lockfile on the
1055	> target arch.
1056	
1057	### TypeScript type generation
1058	
1059	`index.d.ts` is **never hand-written**. The `napi-derive` macro emits type
1060	metadata and the CLI assembles the `.d.ts` at build time — function signatures,
1061	the `AgentResponse` class, `Promise<T>` for async, `T | null` for `Option<T>`.
1062	Where an inferred type is too loose (e.g. the dynamic cell-value arrays), the
1063	wrapper uses `#[napi(ts_arg_type = "...")]` / `#[napi(ts_return_type = "...")]`
1064	overrides so the published types match the hand-authored contract below.
1065	
1066	### Cross-compilation and CI
1067	
1068	`@napi-rs/cli`'s `--cross-compile` flag selects `cargo-zigbuild` as the linker
1069	for non-native Linux/macOS targets (and `cargo-xwin` for Windows). The two
1070	shipped targets build from a single Linux runner:
1071	
1072	```bash
1073	cargo install cargo-zigbuild
1074	napi build --release --cross-compile --target aarch64-apple-darwin
1075	napi build --release --cross-compile --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
1076	```
1077	
1078	The publish CI uses a `fail-fast: false` matrix that builds one `.node` per
1079	target, uploads each as an artifact, then a publish job downloads all artifacts
1080	and runs `napi prepublish`:
1081	
1082	```yaml
1083	strategy:
1084	  fail-fast: false
1085	  matrix:
1086	    include:
1087	      - target: x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
1088	        host: ubuntu-latest
1089	        cross: true            # triggers cargo-zigbuild
1090	      - target: aarch64-apple-darwin
1091	        host: macos-latest     # native build (preferred for code-signing)
1092	```
1093	
1094	The publish job emits the per-platform packages and the main `michi` package
1095	together. The npm package version is asserted equal to the crate version before
1096	publish (see Versioning and release).
1097	
1098	**Windows is a non-goal for v1.** The agent consumers michi targets (MCP
1099	servers, CLIs invoked by coding agents) run on Linux and macOS hosts; a
1100	`windows-x64` target would add `cargo-xwin` tooling and a third CI lane for no
1101	current consumer. It is not blocked on anything — it can be added to the matrix
1102	when a Windows consumer appears.
1103

There's substantial, currently-undocumented drift between the spec and Plan 1's actual implementation, well beyond what the design doc's "Spec updates required" section already flagged.

**The parts that are specifically about MCP v2 already have a well-thought-out answer in the spec — that answer just never got implemented:**

The actual npm package does the opposite — it exports 4 low-level functions (`renderToon`, `emptyState`, `renderHints`, `truncate`) and no `AgentResponse` at all.
- Spec's `AgentResponse` is a rich builder that does the TOON/KV rendering itself (`.items()` → TOON, `.kv_items()` → KV) and has `render_hints_only()`. The actual `AgentResponse` is a thin wrapper around an *already-rendered* body string — you call `toon::render_toon()` yourself first, then hand the result to `AgentResponse::new(body)`. Structurally different, not just renamed.

**Other divergences, not MCP-specific but worth knowing about:**

- `resilience::is_retryable_status` in the actual code retries `500`. The spec explicitly and deliberately excludes it, with a real argument ("retrying write operations that returned 500 may produce duplicate side effects"). This one doesn't look like a deliberate simplification like the others — it looks like drift/an actual bug relative to the spec's own stated reasoning.
- `idempotency` in the spec has hash-based key construction (`IdempotencyKey::from_hash`) and a rich `PartialSuccess` with per-op `FailedOp{reason, recovery}`. The actual code is a bare `Option<String>` check — this is almost certainly *why* my earlier review flagged `IdempotencyKey` as an unused/thin abstraction: it's not over-engineered, it's under-implemented relative to what was speced.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/gabe/.claude/plugins/cache/superpowers-marketplace/superpowers/5.1.0/skills/writing-plans

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## No Placeholders

Every step must contain the actual content an engineer needs. These are **plan failures** — never write them:
- "TBD", "TODO", "implement later", "fill in details"
- "Add appropriate error handling" / "add validation" / "handle edge cases"
- "Write tests for the above" (without actual test code)
- "Similar to Task N" (repeat the code — the engineer may be reading tasks out of order)
- Steps that describe what to do without showing how (code blocks required for code steps)
- References to types, functions, or methods not defined in any task

## Remember
- Exact file paths always
- Complete code in every step — if a step changes code, show the code
- Exact commands with expected output
- DRY, YAGNI, TDD, frequent commits

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Placeholder scan:** Search your plan for red flags — any of the patterns from the "No Placeholders" section above. Fix them.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving the plan, offer execution choice:

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Two execution options:**

**1. Subagent-Driven (recommended)** - I dispatch a fresh subagent per task, review between tasks, fast iteration

**2. Inline Execution** - Execute tasks in this session using executing-plans, batch execution with checkpoints

**Which approach?"**

**If Subagent-Driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development
- Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review

**If Inline Execution chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans
- Batch execution with checkpoints for review

6	## Overview
7	
8	`michi` is a Rust crate of pure agentic response primitives — the
9	conventions that make tools ergonomic for LLMs regardless of protocol or
10	language. It is general-purpose: useful to anyone building AXI-compliant
11	tools, not tied to any specific stack.
12	
13	AXI (Agent eXperience Interface) is a set of ten design principles for
14	agent-ergonomic tooling that treats token budget as a first-class constraint.
15	Its thesis is that the "MCP vs. CLI" debate is the wrong frame: the real
16	question is which design principles make *any* interface effective for an LLM
17	agent. A well-designed interface following these principles measurably
18	outperforms both naive CLIs and MCP on task success rate, cost, duration, and
19	number of turns. `michi` encodes the subset of those principles that are pure,
20	language-agnostic computation — the parts that benefit from a single canonical,
21	tested implementation rather than ad-hoc re-derivation in every tool.
22	
23	It encodes **seven of the ten AXI principles** as typed, tested Rust: TOON
24	list rendering, key-value single-item rendering, contextual disclosure
25	(`help[]`), pre-computed aggregates (`totalCount`), content truncation,

225	## TOON format specification
226	
227	TOON (Token-Optimized Object Notation) is the agent-facing list format.
228	It front-loads structure (type, count, field names) so the LLM has full
229	context before reading any row, then encodes rows as compact comma-separated
230	values. Field names appear once in the header rather than once per row.
231	
232	This is the canonical implementation of **AXI Principle 1 (Token-Efficient
233	Output)**: every token in a response permanently consumes context-window
234	budget, and on multi-turn tasks that cost compounds across turns. TOON omits
235	the braces, quotes, and repeated keys that JSON spends on structure the LLM can
236	already infer positionally.
237	
238	**Why TOON for lists?**
239	Standard JSON repeats field names on every item. Markdown key-value format
240	repeats field names per item, which is ideal for single items and small sets
241	but expensive at scale. TOON trades per-item field repetition for a one-time
242	header, saving proportionally more tokens as N grows. For lists of 5+ items,
243	TOON is the better token budget choice. For single items or small metadata
244	blocks, key-value format remains preferred — see `kv::render_kv()`.
245	
246	AXI's benchmark shows this class of output optimization delivers approximately
247	40% token reduction over equivalent JSON for list data.

249	### Grammar
250	
251	```
252	document     ::= type_header NEWLINE row+ totalcount? help_block?
253	type_header  ::= type_name "[" count "]" "{" field_list "}" ":"
254	type_name    ::= [a-z_][a-z0-9_]*                 (snake_case)
255	count        ::= [0-9]+                            (items in this response)
256	field_list   ::= field_name ("," field_name)*
257	field_name   ::= [a-z_][a-z0-9_]*
258	row          ::= "  " value ("," value)* NEWLINE   (2-space indent)
259	value        ::= scalar | quoted
260	scalar       ::= [^,\n"]*
261	quoted       ::= '"' ( [^"\\] | "\\" . )* '"'     (for values with commas)
262	totalcount   ::= "totalCount: " [0-9]+ NEWLINE     (total available, may exceed count)
263	help_block   ::= "help[" [0-9]+ "]:" NEWLINE hint+
264	hint         ::= "  " [^\n]+ NEWLINE
265	```

305	### Escaping rules
306	
307	- Values containing commas MUST be quoted
308	- Values containing double-quote characters use backslash escape: `\"`
309	- Values containing newlines MUST be truncated before rendering — TOON
310	  does not support multi-line cell values
311	- Null/absent values render as empty scalar: `val1,,val3`
312	- Boolean values: `true` / `false` literals
313	- Numeric values: rendered without quotes
314

350	### `toon` — list rendering for N uniform-schema items
351	
352	TOON is the agent-facing format for lists (**AXI P1**). It front-loads
353	structure (type, count, field names) and encodes rows as compact
354	comma-separated values. Field names appear once in the header rather than once
355	per row. Preferred over key-value format for lists of 5+ items where token
356	savings compound; for single items, use `kv::render_kv()` instead.
357	
358	**Implementation note:** `render_toon()` pre-allocates output capacity via
359	`String::with_capacity` estimated from `items.len() × avg_row_estimate` (see
360	the supplement for the exact heuristic). This is the hot path — no intermediate
361	allocations. The `escape.rs` submodule handles comma/quote escaping inline
362	without heap allocation for the common case (no special characters).
363	
364	```rust
365	pub struct ToonOptions {
366	    /// Max cell value length before inline truncation.
367	    /// Appends "(N chars truncated — use full=true)" when exceeded.
368	    /// Default: 200
369	    pub max_cell_len: usize,
370	    /// Total items available. May exceed rows rendered.
371	    /// Emitted as "totalCount: N" line when Some. This is the canonical
372	    /// AXI P4 (pre-computed aggregate) — it tells the agent how many items
373	    /// exist without forcing a follow-up call.
374	    pub total_count: Option<u64>,
375	}
376	
377	impl Default for ToonOptions { ... }
378	
379	/// Render items as TOON.
380	///
381	/// # Panics (debug only)
382	/// Panics if any `row.len() != fields.len()`.
383	/// In release builds, mismatched rows are silently skipped.
384	///
385	/// Returns empty-state TOON when `items` is empty.
386	pub fn render_toon(
387	    type_name: &str,
388	    items: &[Vec<Value>],
389	    fields: &[&str],
390	    hints: &[Hint],
391	    opts: ToonOptions,
392	) -> String
393	
394	pub enum Value {
395	    Str(String),
396	    Int(i64),
397	    Float(f64),
398	    Bool(bool),
399	    Null,
400	}
401	
402	impl From<&str>           for Value { ... }
403	impl From<String>         for Value { ... }
404	impl From<i64>            for Value { ... }
405	impl From<f64>            for Value { ... }
406	impl From<bool>           for Value { ... }
407	impl From<Option<String>> for Value { ... }
408	```
409	
410	`From<f64>` maps to `Value::Float`; all five scalar variants have a `From`
411	conversion so callers can build rows with `.into()` uniformly.

459	### `hints` — contextual disclosure blocks
460	
461	Implements **AXI Principle 9 (Contextual Disclosure)**: after every output,
462	append a `help[]` section suggesting logical next steps as concrete,
463	parameterized command templates. Carry forward fixed disambiguating flags from
464	the current context, but leave runtime values as named placeholders (`<id>`)
465	rather than guessing them. This eliminates the discovery round trip — the agent
466	sees the next logical actions in the output it just received instead of having
467	to guess subcommands or issue a separate `--help` call.
468	
469	```rust
470	/// A single next-step hint appended after tool output.
471	/// Should be concrete: include tool name and parameter template.
472	///
473	/// Good:  "Call get_issue with number=<number> for full detail"
474	/// Avoid: "Use another tool for more information"
475	pub struct Hint(pub String);

477	impl Hint {
478	    pub fn new(text: impl Into<String>) -> Self
479	}

485	
486	/// Append a help[] block to an existing body string.
487	/// Returns body unchanged when hints is empty.
488	pub fn append_hints(body: &str, hints: &[Hint]) -> String
489	```

493	### `truncate` — size-bounded output with escape hatches
494	
495	Implements **AXI Principle 3 (Content Truncation)**: large text fields are
496	capped to a configurable character limit with a size hint appended that
497	explains the truncation and provides an escape hatch (`use full=true`). A
498	single verbose field can otherwise consume thousands of tokens, exhausting the
499	context budget before the agent has read the rest of a list; truncation
500	preserves enough signal for most operations while reserving budget for
501	subsequent turns.

510	}

546	### `error` — structured errors with exit codes
547	
548	Implements **AXI Principle 6 (Structured Errors and Exit Codes)**: errors are
549	written to **stdout** (not stderr), carry a clean exit code (`0` success, `1`
550	error), carry recovery hints, and never block on interactive prompts. Agents
551	cannot answer `Are you sure? [y/n]`, may not capture stderr at all, and cannot
552	reliably parse freeform error text. `AxiError` encodes the structured contract
553	as a type.
554	
555	The HTTP status → `ErrorCode` mapping is NOT in michi — callers produce an
556	`ErrorCode` after interpreting whatever failure occurred. This keeps the
557	module free of HTTP knowledge.
558	
559	```rust
560	#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
561	pub struct AxiError {
562	    pub code:        ErrorCode,
563	    pub message:     String,
564	    pub hints:       Vec<Hint>,
565	    pub recovery:    Option<RecoveryHint>,
566	    pub retryable:   bool,
567	    pub retry_after: Option<std::time::Duration>,
568	}
569	
570	impl std::fmt::Display for AxiError {
571	    // delegates to render()
572	}
573	
574	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
575	pub enum ErrorCode {
576	    // Non-retryable — agent should not retry without changing params
577	    InvalidInput,    // bad parameters
578	    NotFound,        // resource absent
579	    Unauthorized,    // auth failure
580	    Forbidden,       // permission denied
581	    Conflict,        // resource state mismatch
582	
583	    // Retryable — agent may retry same call
584	    RateLimited,     // 429 — check retry_after
585	    Unavailable,     // 503
586	    Timeout,         // request timed out
587	    ExternalFailure, // downstream error
588	}
589	
590	impl AxiError {
591	    pub fn new(code: ErrorCode, message: impl Into<String>) -> Self
592	    pub fn hint(mut self, hint: impl Into<String>) -> Self
593	    pub fn recovery(mut self, r: RecoveryHint) -> Self
594	    pub fn retry_after(mut self, d: std::time::Duration) -> Self
595	
596	    /// Render to stdout-ready string with hints attached.
597	    pub fn render(&self) -> String
598	
599	    /// AXI exit codes: 0 = success/already_done, 1 = all other errors.
600	    /// Callers should not invent additional codes.
601	    pub fn exit_code(&self) -> i32
602	}
603	```
604	
605	The `thiserror::Error` derive plus the `Display` impl (which delegates to
606	`render()`) make `AxiError` usable with `?` in ordinary Rust call sites.
607	`ErrorCode` is `Copy + Eq` so callers can match and compare it freely.
608	
609	`ErrorCode` renders as snake_case. `render()` produces a KV-shaped block on
610	stdout, e.g. for `AxiError::new(ErrorCode::NotFound, "Issue #9999 does not
611	exist in this repository").hint("Call list_issues to see available numbers")`:
612	
613	```

615	message: Issue #9999 does not exist in this repository
616	exit_code: 1
617	help[1]:
618	  Call list_issues to see available numbers
619	```
